**Tafsir of Surah al-Rum (Chapter of the Romans)**

Surah al-Rum is entirely Meccan, without any disagreement, and it has sixty verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Alif. Lam. Mim. (1) The Romans have been defeated (2) in the nearest part of the land, but after their defeat they will overcome (3) within a few years. The command belongs to Allah, before and after. On that day the believers will rejoice (4) in the victory of Allah. He gives victory to whom He wills, and He is the Mighty, the Merciful. (5)

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim. The Romans have been defeated in the nearest part of the land﴾. Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "When the Day of Badr came, the Romans prevailed over the Persians, and this pleased the believers. Then this was revealed: 'Alif. Lam. Mim. The Romans have been defeated in the nearest part of the land... to His words... the believers will rejoice in the victory of Allah.'" He said: "So the believers rejoiced at the Romans' victory over the Persians." Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a gharib (singular) hadith from this route." Nasr ibn 'Ali al-Jahdhami recited it as "Ghulibat al-Rum" (The Romans have been defeated).

He also narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas, in a more complete form. Ibn 'Abbas said regarding the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, "Alif. Lam. Mim. The Romans have been defeated in the nearest part of the land," he said: "They were defeated, and they defeated (others)." He said: "The polytheists loved that the people of Persia would prevail over the Romans, because they and the Persians were people of idols. The Muslims loved that the Romans would prevail over the Persians, because they were people of a Book. They mentioned this to Abu Bakr, and Abu Bakr mentioned it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He said: 'Indeed they will overcome.' Abu Bakr told them this, and they said: 'Set a term between us and you. If we prevail, we will receive such-and-such, and if you prevail, you will receive such-and-such.' So he set the term at five years, but they did not prevail. This was mentioned to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'Why did you not make it less than that?' (I think he said: 'ten.')" Abu Sa'id said: "And al-bid' is less than ten." He said: "Then the Romans prevailed afterward, and that is His words: 'Alif. Lam. Mim. The Romans have been defeated... the believers will rejoice in the victory of Allah.'"

Sufyan said: "I heard that they prevailed over them on the Day of Badr." Abu 'Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: "This is a hasan sahih gharib hadith."

He also narrated it from Niyar ibn Mukram al-Aslami, who said: "When the verses were revealed, 'Alif. Lam. Mim. The Romans have been defeated in the nearest part of the land, and after their defeat they will overcome, within a few years,' the Persians were prevailing over the Romans on the day these verses were revealed. The Muslims loved the Romans' victory over them, because they and the Romans were people of a Book. In this regard Allah the Exalted revealed: 'And on that day the believers will rejoice in the victory of Allah. He gives victory to whom He wills, and He is the Mighty, the Merciful.' The Quraysh loved the Persians' victory, because they and the Persians were not people of a Book nor did they believe in resurrection. When Allah revealed this verse, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) went out shouting in the outskirts of Mecca: 'Alif. Lam. Mim. The Romans have been defeated in the nearest part of the land, and after their defeat they will overcome, within a few years.' Some of the Quraysh said to Abu Bakr: 'That is between us and you. Your companion claims that the Romans will overcome the Persians within a few years! Shall we wager you on that?' He said: 'Yes.' This was before the prohibition of gambling (rihan). So Abu Bakr and the polytheists made the wager and agreed on its terms. They said to Abu Bakr: 'How many years do you set for the bid'? Three years or nine years? Name a middle term between us and you that you will accept.' They fixed the term at six years. He said: 'Six years passed before they prevailed. So the polytheists took Abu Bakr's pledge. When the seventh year came, the Romans prevailed over the Persians. The Muslims criticized Abu Bakr for setting six years, and he said: "Because Allah the Exalted said, 'within a few years.'" At that time many people embraced Islam.'" Abu 'Isa said: "This is a hasan sahih gharib hadith."

Al-Qushayri, Ibn 'Atiyya and others narrated: "When the verses were revealed, Abu Bakr went out with them to the polytheists and said: 'Does it please you that the Romans have been defeated? Indeed our Prophet informed us from Allah, Exalted, that they will overcome within a few years.' Ubayy ibn Khalaf and his brother Umayya (and it was said Abu Sufyan ibn Harb) said to him: 'O Abu Fasil!' [[al-fasil: the young camel when it is weaned from its mother.]] (they were alluding to his kunya, 'O Abu Bakr'), 'Let us bet on it,' that is, let us wager on this matter. So Abu Bakr made the wager with them. Qatada said: 'That was before gambling (al-qimar) was prohibited.' They made the stake five she-camels (qala'is) [[al-qala'is: plural of qulus, meaning young she-camels.]] and the term three years. It was also said: they made the stake three she-camels. Then he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him, and he said: 'Why did you not seek a safer margin? For al-bid' is what lies between three and nine, or ten! But go back, increase the stake for them, and ask them to extend the term.' Abu Bakr did so. They made the she-camels one hundred and the term nine years, and the Romans prevailed during the term." Al-Sha'bi said: "They prevailed within nine years."

Al-Qushayri said: "The well-known report is that the Romans' victory came in the seventh year after the Persians' defeat of the Romans. Perhaps al-Sha'bi's report is a copyist's error, from seven (sab') to nine (tis')." In some reports: "He made the she-camels seven, up to nine years." It is said that this was the last of the conquests of Khusraw Abarwiz, in which he conquered Constantinople until he built in it the House of Fire. He informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this grieved him, so Allah the Exalted revealed these two verses.

Al-Naqqash and others narrated: "When Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) wished to emigrate with the Prophet (ﷺ), Ubayy ibn Khalaf seized him and said: 'Give me a guarantor for the stake [[al-khatar (with a vowel on the first letter): the pledge and what one stakes in a wager.]] in case you are defeated.' So his son 'Abd al-Rahman stood surety for him. When Ubayy wished to set out for Uhud, 'Abd al-Rahman asked him for the guarantee, and he gave him a guarantor. Then Ubayy died in Mecca from a wound that the Prophet (ﷺ) had inflicted on him. The Romans prevailed over the Persians on the Day of Hudaybiyya, nine years after their wager."

Al-Sha'bi said: "That period had not passed before the Romans defeated the Persians. They tethered their horses at al-Mada'in and built Rumiyya. Then Abu Bakr won the wager from Ubayy and took the stake from his heirs. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'Give it away in charity,' and he gave it in charity." [[Qamar: to defeat someone.]]

The exegetes said: The cause of the Romans' defeat of the Persians was a woman among the Persians who gave birth only to kings and heroes. Khusraw said to her: "I wish to appoint one of your sons over an army that I will equip against the Romans." She said: "This is Hurmuz, who is craftier than a fox and more wary than a hawk. This is Farrukhan, who is sharper than a spear and more piercing than an arrow. And this is Shahrbaraz [[This is how it appears in the books of tafsir. What is in the Tarikh al-Tabari is: Shahrabaraz.]], who is more forbearing than such-and-such. Choose." He chose the forbearing one and appointed him, and he marched to the Romans with the people of Persia, and he prevailed over the Romans.

'Ikrima and others said: When Shahrbaraz defeated the Romans, he devastated their lands until he reached the Gulf. His brother Farrukhan said: "I saw myself sitting on the throne of Khusraw." Khusraw wrote to Shahrbaraz: "Send me the head of Farrukhan," but he did not do it. Khusraw wrote to the people of Persia: "I have appointed Farrukhan over you and dismissed Shahrbaraz." And he wrote to Farrukhan that when he took command he should kill Shahrbaraz. Farrukhan wished to kill Shahrbaraz, so Shahrbaraz brought out three letters from Khusraw ordering him to kill Farrukhan. Shahrbaraz said to Farrukhan: "Khusraw wrote to me three times to kill you, and each time I refused and argued with him about you. Will you kill me on the strength of a single letter?" So Farrukhan returned the kingship to his brother. Shahrbaraz wrote to Caesar, the king of the Romans, and they cooperated against Khusraw. The Romans defeated the Persians, and Khusraw died.

The news reached the Prophet (ﷺ) on the Day of Hudaybiyya, and the Muslims with him rejoiced. This is the meaning of His words, the Exalted: ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim. The Romans have been defeated in the nearest part of the land﴾, meaning the land of al-Sham (Syria). 'Ikrima said: "Adhri'at," which is the area between the lands of the Arabs and al-Sham. It was also said: Caesar had sent a man called Yahannas, and Khusraw sent Shahrbaraz, and they met at Adhri'at and Busra, which are the nearest lands of al-Sham to the land of the Arabs and the non-Arabs. Mujahid said: "Al-Jazira," which is a place between Iraq and al-Sham. Muqatil said: "Al-Urdunn and Filastin." "Adna" means "nearer."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "If the battle took place at Adhri'at, then it is from the nearest of the land in comparison with Mecca, and it is what Imru' al-Qays mentioned in his words:

*I passed by her from Adhri'at, and her people
at Yathrib, the nearest of her dwellings, a high vantage point.*

If the battle took place in the Peninsula, then by measure it is nearer to the land of Kisra; and if it took place in Jordan, then it is nearer to the land of the Romans. When that happened and the Romans were defeated, the disbelievers rejoiced. So Allah gave His servants the good news that the Romans would be victorious and that the dominion would belong to them in the war. The discussion of the openings of the surahs has already passed.

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah read *ghuliba al-Rum* (غُلِبَتِ الرُّومُ) with a fatha on the ghayn and the lam. The interpretation of this is that what occurred on the Day of Badr was that the Romans had been defeated, which grieved the disbelievers of Quraysh, and the Muslims rejoiced at it. So Allah the Exalted gave His servants the good news that they too would be victorious within a few years. Abu Hatim mentioned this interpretation.

Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: The reading of most people is *ghulibat al-Rum* (غُلِبَتِ الرُّومُ) with a damma on the ghayn and a kasra on the lam. It is related from Ibn 'Umar and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that they read *ghulibat al-Rum* and read *sa-yughlabun* (سَيُغْلَبُونَ). Abu Hatim relates that 'Ismah narrated from Harun that this is the reading of the people of al-Sham, but Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: "This 'Ismah is weak," while Abu Hatim relates much from him. The hadith indicates that the reading is *ghulibat* with a damma on the ghayn. In this report there is evidence for the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), because the Romans had been defeated by the Persians; Allah the Mighty and Majestic informed His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) that the Romans would overcome the Persians within a few years, and that the believers would rejoice at that, because the Romans were People of the Book. So this was from the knowledge of the unseen which Allah the Mighty and Majestic informed of, which they had not known [[addition from al-Nahhas.]]. He also commanded Abu Bakr to bet with them on that and to go to the limit in the wager. Then wagering was afterwards forbidden and abrogated by the prohibition of gambling.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The reading with a damma on the ghayn is more sound. The people are agreed on *sa-yaghlibun* (سَيَغْلِبُونَ) with a fatha on the ya', meaning the Romans. It is narrated from Ibn 'Umar that he also read with a damma on the ya' in *sa-yughlabun* (سَيُغْلَبُونَ) [[In K: with a fatha on the ya'.]]. In this reading there is an inversion of the meaning on which the reports are consistent.

Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: For whoever reads *sa-yughlabun*, the meaning in his view is: "And the Persians, after their defeat, will be defeated," that is, after they had been victorious, they will be defeated. It is related that the Romans' attack on the Persians was on the Day of Badr, as in the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri in the hadith of al-Tirmidhi. It is also related that it was on the day of Hudaybiyah, and that the news reached them on the day of the Pledge of al-Ridwan; this was said by 'Ikrimah and Qatadah. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: On both days there was victory from Allah for the believers.

People have mentioned that the cause of the Muslims' joy at the victory of the Romans, and their concern that they might be defeated, is only that the Romans are People of the Book like the Muslims, while the Persians are of the idol-worshippers, as has been explained previously in the hadith [[In Sh: (like the Muslims; they are closer than the people of idols ...).]]. Al-Nahhas said: Another view, and it is more preferable, is that their joy was only for the fulfilment of the promise of Allah the Exalted, since in it there was evidence of prophethood, for He, blessed and exalted, informed of what would happen within a few years, and so it came to pass.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It seems that this may be explained by what consideration requires, namely the love that the lesser enemy be defeated, since it is less burdensome, whereas when the greater one is defeated, fear of it increases. So reflect on this meaning, together with what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) hoped for: the manifestation of his religion and of the law of Allah with which He sent him, his dominance over the nations, and the desire of the disbelievers of Makkah that Allah would strike him with a king who would uproot him and relieve them of him.

It was also said: Their joy was only at the victory of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) over the polytheists, because Jibril informed the Prophet, peace be upon him, of that on the Day of Badr; this was related by al-Qushayri.

I say: It is possible that their joy was at the whole of that: they rejoiced at their own victory over their enemy, at the victory of the Romans too, and at the fulfilment of the promise of Allah.

Abu Haywah al-Shami and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqa read *min ba'di ghalbihim* (مِنْ بَعْدِ غَلْبِهِمْ) with a sukun on the lam, and both are dialectal forms, like *al-za'n* and *al-za'n* (الظَّعَنِ وَالظَّعْنِ). Al-Farra' claimed that the original was *min ba'di ghalabatihim* (مِنْ بَعْدِ غَلَبَتِهِمْ), so the ta' was deleted, as it was deleted in the Exalted's saying *wa-aqama al-salat* (وَأَقامَ الصَّلاةَ), whose original is *wa-iqamat al-salat* (وَإِقَامَةُ الصَّلَاةِ). Al-Nahhas said: This is an error that would not be confusing to many of the grammarians, because *aqama al-salat* is a verbal noun from which something has been deleted because its verb is defective, so the ta' was made a substitute for the deleted element, whereas *ghalaba* is not defective, and nothing has been deleted from it. Al-Asma'i has related: *tarada tardan* (طَرَدَ طَرَدًا), *jalaba jalban* (جَلَبَ جَلَبًا), *halaba halban* (حَلَبَ حَلَبًا), and *ghalaba ghalban* (غَلَبَ غَلَبًا). So where is the deletion in this, and is it permissible to say of *akala aklan* (أَكَلَ أَكْلًا) and what resembles it that something has been deleted from it?

(*Fi bid'i sinin*) (فِي بِضْعِ سِنِينَ): The ha' is deleted from *bid'* (بِضْعِ) to distinguish the masculine from the feminine, and the discussion of this has already passed in *Yusuf* [[See vol. 9, p. 197.]]. The nun of *sinin* (سِنِينَ) is given a fatha because it is a sound plural. Among the Arabs there are those who say *fi bid'i sinin* as they say *fi ghislin* (فِي غِسْلِينٍ). It is permissible to pluralise *sanah* (سَنَةٌ) with the sound masculine plural, with the waw and nun or the ya' and nun, because something has been deleted from it, so this plural was made a substitute for the deficiency in its singular. The original of *sanah* is *sanhah* or *sanwah*, and the sin was given a kasra in it to show that its plural lies outside its analogy and pattern. This is the view of the Basrans. Al-Farra' would be obliged to give it a damma, because he says that the damma is an indicator of the waw, and a waw has been deleted from *sanah* according to one of the two views; yet no one that we know of has given it a damma.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿To Allah belongs the command, before and after﴾. He, the Exalted, informed that He alone has the power, and that whatever victory or other matter exists in the world comes only from Him, by His will and His power. So He said: "To Allah belongs the command," meaning the execution of decrees.

"Before and after" means before this victory and after it. It was also said: before everything and after everything. *Min qablu wa-min ba'du* (مِنْ قَبْلُ وَمِنْ بَعْدُ) are two adverbs of place or time that were built on the damma, because they are defined by the deletion of what they are attached to, and they became containing what has been deleted, so they differed from the definition of nouns and resembled particles in containing [meaning]; so they were built, and they were specially given the damma because of their resemblance to the singular vocative, in that when it is made indefinite and is annexed its indeclinability ceases, and likewise these two, so they were given a damma. It is said: *min qablu wa-min ba'du*. Al-Kisa'i related from some of the Banu Asad: *lillahi al-amru min qablu wa-min ba'du*, with the first in the genitive and nunated, and the second in the damma without nunation. Al-Farra' related *min qabli wa-min ba'di* in the genitive without nunation. Al-Nahhas denied this and rejected it. Al-Farra' said in his book: "There are many things in the Qur'an whose error is evident, among them that he claimed it is permissible to say *min qabli wa-min ba'di*, whereas it is only permissible to say *min qablu wa-min ba'du* on the basis that they are indefinite." Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is "from what precedes and from what follows."

(*Wa-yawma'idhin yafrahu al-mu'minun bi-nasri Allah*) (وَيَوْمَئِذٍ يَفْرَحُ الْمُؤْمِنُونَ بِنَصْرِ اللَّهِ): this has already been mentioned.

(*Yansuru man yasha'*) (يَنْصُرُ مَنْ يَشاءُ): meaning from among His allies, because His victory is specific to the victory of His allies over their enemies. As for the victory of His enemies over His allies, that is not His victory; it is only a trial, though it may be called a triumph.

(*Wa-huwa al-'Aziz*) (وَهُوَ الْعَزِيزُ) in His retribution, (*al-Rahim*) (الرَّحِيمُ) toward those who obey Him.

**Tafsir of Surah al-Rum (Chapter of the Romans)**

He said: "So the believers rejoiced at the Romans' victory over the Persians." Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a gharib (singular) hadith from this route." Nasr ibn 'Ali al-Jahdhami recited it as "Ghulibat al-Rum" (The Romans have been defeated).

He also narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas, in a more complete form. Ibn 'Abbas said regarding the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, "Alif. Lam. Mim. The Romans have been defeated in the nearest part of the land," he said: "They were defeated, and they defeated (others)." The Muslims loved that the Romans would prevail over the Persians, because they were people of a Book. They mentioned this to Abu Bakr, and Abu Bakr mentioned it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He said: 'Indeed they will overcome.' Abu Bakr told them this, and they said: 'Set a term between us and you. If we prevail, we will receive such-and-such, and if you prevail, you will receive such-and-such.' So he set the term at five years, but they did not prevail. This was mentioned to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'Why did you not make it less than that?' (I think he said: 'ten.')" Abu Sa'id said: "And al-bid' is less than ten." **Tafsir of Surah al-Rum (Chapter of the Romans)**

Surah al-Rum is entirely Meccan, without any disagreement, and it has sixty verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Alif. Lam. Mim. (1) The Romans have been defeated (2) in the nearest part of the land, but after their defeat they will overcome (3) within a few years. The command belongs to Allah, before and after. On that day the believers will rejoice (4) in the victory of Allah. He gives victory to whom He wills, and He is the Mighty, the Merciful. (5)

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim. The Romans have been defeated in the nearest part of the land﴾. Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "When the Day of Badr came, the Romans prevailed over the Persians, and this pleased the believers. Then this was revealed: 'Alif. Lam. Mim. The Romans have been defeated in the nearest part of the land... to His words... the believers will rejoice in the victory of Allah.'" He said: "So the believers rejoiced at the Romans' victory over the Persians." Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a gharib (singular) hadith from this route." Nasr ibn 'Ali al-Jahdhami recited it as "Ghulibat al-Rum" (The Romans have been defeated).

He also narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas, in a more complete form. Ibn 'Abbas said regarding the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, "Alif. Lam. Mim. The Romans have been defeated in the nearest part of the land," he said: "They were defeated, and they defeated (others)." He said: "The polytheists loved that the people of Persia would prevail over the Romans, because they and the Persians were people of idols. The Muslims loved that the Romans would prevail over the Persians, because they were people of a Book. They mentioned this to Abu Bakr, and Abu Bakr mentioned it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He said: 'Indeed they will overcome.' Abu Bakr told them this, and they said: 'Set a term between us and you. If we prevail, we will receive such-and-such, and if you prevail, you will receive such-and-such.' So he set the term at five years, but they did not prevail. This was mentioned to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'Why did you not make it less than that?' (I think he said: 'ten.')" Abu Sa'id said: "And al-bid' is less than ten." He said: "Then the Romans prevailed afterward, and that is His words: 'Alif. Lam. Mim. The Romans have been defeated... the believers will rejoice in the victory of Allah.'"

Sufyan said: "I heard that they prevailed over them on the Day of Badr." Abu 'Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: "This is a hasan sahih gharib hadith."

He also narrated it from Niyar ibn Mukram al-Aslami, who said: "When the verses were revealed, 'Alif. Lam. Mim. The Romans have been defeated in the nearest part of the land, and after their defeat they will overcome, within a few years,' the Persians were prevailing over the Romans on the day these verses were revealed. The Muslims loved the Romans' victory over them, because they and the Romans were people of a Book. In this regard Allah the Exalted revealed: 'And on that day the believers will rejoice in the victory of Allah. He gives victory to whom He wills, and He is the Mighty, the Merciful.' The Quraysh loved the Persians' victory, because they and the Persians were not people of a Book nor did they believe in resurrection. When Allah revealed this verse, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) went out shouting in the outskirts of Mecca: 'Alif. Lam. Mim. The Romans have been defeated in the nearest part of the land, and after their defeat they will overcome, within a few years.' Some of the Quraysh said to Abu Bakr: 'That is between us and you. Your companion claims that the Romans will overcome the Persians within a few years! Shall we wager you on that?' He said: 'Yes.' This was before the prohibition of gambling (rihan). So Abu Bakr and the polytheists made the wager and agreed on its terms. They said to Abu Bakr: 'How many years do you set for the bid'? Three years or nine years? Name a middle term between us and you that you will accept.' They fixed the term at six years. He said: 'Six years passed before they prevailed. So the polytheists took Abu Bakr's pledge. When the seventh year came, the Romans prevailed over the Persians. The Muslims criticized Abu Bakr for setting six years, and he said: "Because Allah the Exalted said, 'within a few years.'" At that time many people embraced Islam.'" Abu 'Isa said: "This is a hasan sahih gharib hadith."

Al-Qushayri, Ibn 'Atiyya and others narrated: "When the verses were revealed, Abu Bakr went out with them to the polytheists and said: 'Does it please you that the Romans have been defeated? Indeed our Prophet informed us from Allah, Exalted, that they will overcome within a few years.' So Abu Bakr made the wager with them. Qatada said: 'That was before gambling (al-qimar) was prohibited.' They made the stake five she-camels (qala'is) [[al-qala'is: plural of qulus, meaning young she-camels.]] and the term three years. It was also said: they made the stake three she-camels. Then he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him, and he said: 'Why did you not seek a safer margin? For al-bid' is what lies between three and nine, or ten! Al-Sha'bi said: "They prevailed within nine years."

Al-Qushayri said: "The well-known report is that the Romans' victory came in the seventh year after the Persians' defeat of the Romans. Khusraw said to her: "I wish to appoint one of your sons over an army that I will equip against the Romans." She said: "This is Hurmuz, who is craftier than a fox and more wary than a hawk. *I passed by her from Adhri'at, and her people
at Yathrib, the nearest of her dwellings, a high vantage point.*

If the battle took place in the Peninsula, then by measure it is nearer to the land of Kisra; and if it took place in Jordan, then it is nearer to the land of the Romans. The Muslims loved the Romans' victory over them, because they and the Romans were people of a Book. In this regard Allah the Exalted revealed: 'And on that day the believers will rejoice in the victory of Allah. He gives victory to whom He wills, and He is the Mighty, the Merciful.' The Quraysh loved the Persians' victory, because they and the Persians were not people of a Book nor did they believe in resurrection. When Allah revealed this verse, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) went out shouting in the outskirts of Mecca: 'Alif. Lam. Mim. The Romans have been defeated in the nearest part of the land, and after their defeat they will overcome, within a few years.' Some of the Quraysh said to Abu Bakr: 'That is between us and you. Your companion claims that the Romans will overcome the Persians within a few years! Shall we wager you on that?' He said: 'Yes.' This was before the prohibition of gambling (rihan). So Abu Bakr and the polytheists made the wager and agreed on its terms. They said to Abu Bakr: 'How many years do you set for the bid'? Three years or nine years? Name a middle term between us and you that you will accept.' They fixed the term at six years. He said: 'Six years passed before they prevailed. So the polytheists took Abu Bakr's pledge. When the seventh year came, the Romans prevailed over the Persians. The Muslims criticized Abu Bakr for setting six years, and he said: "Because Allah the Exalted said, 'within a few years.'" At that time many people embraced Islam.'" Abu 'Isa said: "This is a hasan sahih gharib hadith."

Al-Qushayri, Ibn 'Atiyya and others narrated: "When the verses were revealed, Abu Bakr went out with them to the polytheists and said: 'Does it please you that the Romans have been defeated? Indeed our Prophet informed us from Allah, Exalted, that they will overcome within a few years.' Ubayy ibn Khalaf and his brother Umayya (and it was said Abu Sufyan ibn Harb) said to him: 'O Abu Fasil!' [[al-fasil: the young camel when it is weaned from its mother.]] (they were alluding to his kunya, 'O Abu Bakr'), 'Let us bet on it,' that is, let us wager on this matter. So Abu Bakr made the wager with them. Qatada said: 'That was before gambling (al-qimar) was prohibited.' They made the stake five she-camels (qala'is) [[al-qala'is: plural of qulus, meaning young she-camels.]] and the term three years. It was also said: they made the stake three she-camels. Then he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him, and he said: 'Why did you not seek a safer margin? For al-bid' is what lies between three and nine, or ten! But go back, increase the stake for them, and ask them to extend the term.' Abu Bakr did so. They made the she-camels one hundred and the term nine years, and the Romans prevailed during the term." Al-Sha'bi said: "They prevailed within nine years."

Al-Qushayri said: "The well-known report is that the Romans' victory came in the seventh year after the Persians' defeat of the Romans. Perhaps al-Sha'bi's report is a copyist's error, from seven (sab') to nine (tis')." In some reports: "He made the she-camels seven, up to nine years." It is said that this was the last of the conquests of Khusraw Abarwiz, in which he conquered Constantinople until he built in it the House of Fire. He informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this grieved him, so Allah the Exalted revealed these two verses.

Al-Naqqash and others narrated: "When Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) wished to emigrate with the Prophet (ﷺ), Ubayy ibn Khalaf seized him and said: 'Give me a guarantor for the stake [[al-khatar (with a vowel on the first letter): the pledge and what one stakes in a wager.]] in case you are defeated.' So his son 'Abd al-Rahman stood surety for him. When Ubayy wished to set out for Uhud, 'Abd al-Rahman asked him for the guarantee, and he gave him a guarantor. Then Ubayy died in Mecca from a wound that the Prophet (ﷺ) had inflicted on him. The Romans prevailed over the Persians on the Day of Hudaybiyya, nine years after their wager."

Al-Sha'bi said: "That period had not passed before the Romans defeated the Persians. They tethered their horses at al-Mada'in and built Rumiyya. Then Abu Bakr won the wager from Ubayy and took the stake from his heirs. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'Give it away in charity,' and he gave it in charity." [[Qamar: to defeat someone.]]

The exegetes said: The cause of the Romans' defeat of the Persians was a woman among the Persians who gave birth only to kings and heroes. Khusraw said to her: "I wish to appoint one of your sons over an army that I will equip against the Romans." She said: "This is Hurmuz, who is craftier than a fox and more wary than a hawk. This is Farrukhan, who is sharper than a spear and more piercing than an arrow. And this is Shahrbaraz [[This is how it appears in the books of tafsir. What is in the Tarikh al-Tabari is: Shahrabaraz.]], who is more forbearing than such-and-such. Choose." He chose the forbearing one and appointed him, and he marched to the Romans with the people of Persia, and he prevailed over the Romans.

'Ikrima and others said: When Shahrbaraz defeated the Romans, he devastated their lands until he reached the Gulf. His brother Farrukhan said: "I saw myself sitting on the throne of Khusraw." Khusraw wrote to Shahrbaraz: "Send me the head of Farrukhan," but he did not do it. Khusraw wrote to the people of Persia: "I have appointed Farrukhan over you and dismissed Shahrbaraz." And he wrote to Farrukhan that when he took command he should kill Shahrbaraz. Farrukhan wished to kill Shahrbaraz, so Shahrbaraz brought out three letters from Khusraw ordering him to kill Farrukhan. Shahrbaraz said to Farrukhan: "Khusraw wrote to me three times to kill you, and each time I refused and argued with him about you. Will you kill me on the strength of a single letter?" So Farrukhan returned the kingship to his brother. Shahrbaraz wrote to Caesar, the king of the Romans, and they cooperated against Khusraw. The Romans defeated the Persians, and Khusraw died.

The news reached the Prophet (ﷺ) on the Day of Hudaybiyya, and the Muslims with him rejoiced. This is the meaning of His words, the Exalted: ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim. The Romans have been defeated in the nearest part of the land﴾, meaning the land of al-Sham (Syria). 'Ikrima said: "Adhri'at," which is the area between the lands of the Arabs and al-Sham. It was also said: Caesar had sent a man called Yahannas, and Khusraw sent Shahrbaraz, and they met at Adhri'at and Busra, which are the nearest lands of al-Sham to the land of the Arabs and the non-Arabs. Mujahid said: "Al-Jazira," which is a place between Iraq and al-Sham. Muqatil said: "Al-Urdunn and Filastin." "Adna" means "nearer."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "If the battle took place at Adhri'at, then it is from the nearest of the land in comparison with Mecca, and it is what Imru' al-Qays mentioned in his words:

*I passed by her from Adhri'at, and her people
at Yathrib, the nearest of her dwellings, a high vantage point.*

If the battle took place in the Peninsula, then by measure it is nearer to the land of Kisra; and if it took place in Jordan, then it is nearer to the land of the Romans. When that happened and the Romans were defeated, the disbelievers rejoiced. So Allah gave His servants the good news that the Romans would be victorious and that the dominion would belong to them in the war. The discussion of the openings of the surahs has already passed.

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah read *ghuliba al-Rum* (غُلِبَتِ الرُّومُ) with a fatha on the ghayn and the lam. The interpretation of this is that what occurred on the Day of Badr was that the Romans had been defeated, which grieved the disbelievers of Quraysh, and the Muslims rejoiced at it. So Allah the Exalted gave His servants the good news that they too would be victorious within a few years. Abu Hatim mentioned this interpretation.

Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: The reading of most people is *ghulibat al-Rum* (غُلِبَتِ الرُّومُ) with a damma on the ghayn and a kasra on the lam. It is related from Ibn 'Umar and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that they read *ghulibat al-Rum* and read *sa-yughlabun* (سَيُغْلَبُونَ). Abu Hatim relates that 'Ismah narrated from Harun that this is the reading of the people of al-Sham, but Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: "This 'Ismah is weak," while Abu Hatim relates much from him. The hadith indicates that the reading is *ghulibat* with a damma on the ghayn. In this report there is evidence for the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), because the Romans had been defeated by the Persians; Allah the Mighty and Majestic informed His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) that the Romans would overcome the Persians within a few years, and that the believers would rejoice at that, because the Romans were People of the Book. So this was from the knowledge of the unseen which Allah the Mighty and Majestic informed of, which they had not known [[addition from al-Nahhas.]]. He also commanded Abu Bakr to bet with them on that and to go to the limit in the wager. Then wagering was afterwards forbidden and abrogated by the prohibition of gambling.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The reading with a damma on the ghayn is more sound. The people are agreed on *sa-yaghlibun* (سَيَغْلِبُونَ) with a fatha on the ya', meaning the Romans. It is narrated from Ibn 'Umar that he also read with a damma on the ya' in *sa-yughlabun* (سَيُغْلَبُونَ) [[In K: with a fatha on the ya'.]]. In this reading there is an inversion of the meaning on which the reports are consistent.

Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: For whoever reads *sa-yughlabun*, the meaning in his view is: "And the Persians, after their defeat, will be defeated," that is, after they had been victorious, they will be defeated. It is related that the Romans' attack on the Persians was on the Day of Badr, as in the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri in the hadith of al-Tirmidhi. It is also related that it was on the day of Hudaybiyah, and that the news reached them on the day of the Pledge of al-Ridwan; this was said by 'Ikrimah and Qatadah. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: On both days there was victory from Allah for the believers.

People have mentioned that the cause of the Muslims' joy at the victory of the Romans, and their concern that they might be defeated, is only that the Romans are People of the Book like the Muslims, while the Persians are of the idol-worshippers, as has been explained previously in the hadith [[In Sh: (like the Muslims; they are closer than the people of idols ...).]]. Al-Nahhas said: Another view, and it is more preferable, is that their joy was only for the fulfilment of the promise of Allah the Exalted, since in it there was evidence of prophethood, for He, blessed and exalted, informed of what would happen within a few years, and so it came to pass.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It seems that this may be explained by what consideration requires, namely the love that the lesser enemy be defeated, since it is less burdensome, whereas when the greater one is defeated, fear of it increases. So reflect on this meaning, together with what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) hoped for: the manifestation of his religion and of the law of Allah with which He sent him, his dominance over the nations, and the desire of the disbelievers of Makkah that Allah would strike him with a king who would uproot him and relieve them of him.

It was also said: Their joy was only at the victory of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) over the polytheists, because Jibril informed the Prophet, peace be upon him, of that on the Day of Badr; this was related by al-Qushayri.

I say: It is possible that their joy was at the whole of that: they rejoiced at their own victory over their enemy, at the victory of the Romans too, and at the fulfilment of the promise of Allah.

Abu Haywah al-Shami and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqa read *min ba'di ghalbihim* (مِنْ بَعْدِ غَلْبِهِمْ) with a sukun on the lam, and both are dialectal forms, like *al-za'n* and *al-za'n* (الظَّعَنِ وَالظَّعْنِ). Al-Farra' claimed that the original was *min ba'di ghalabatihim* (مِنْ بَعْدِ غَلَبَتِهِمْ), so the ta' was deleted, as it was deleted in the Exalted's saying *wa-aqama al-salat* (وَأَقامَ الصَّلاةَ), whose original is *wa-iqamat al-salat* (وَإِقَامَةُ الصَّلَاةِ). Al-Nahhas said: This is an error that would not be confusing to many of the grammarians, because *aqama al-salat* is a verbal noun from which something has been deleted because its verb is defective, so the ta' was made a substitute for the deleted element, whereas *ghalaba* is not defective, and nothing has been deleted from it. Al-Asma'i has related: *tarada tardan* (طَرَدَ طَرَدًا), *jalaba jalban* (جَلَبَ جَلَبًا), *halaba halban* (حَلَبَ حَلَبًا), and *ghalaba ghalban* (غَلَبَ غَلَبًا). So where is the deletion in this, and is it permissible to say of *akala aklan* (أَكَلَ أَكْلًا) and what resembles it that something has been deleted from it?

(*Fi bid'i sinin*) (فِي بِضْعِ سِنِينَ): The ha' is deleted from *bid'* (بِضْعِ) to distinguish the masculine from the feminine, and the discussion of this has already passed in *Yusuf* [[See vol. 9, p. 197.]]. The nun of *sinin* (سِنِينَ) is given a fatha because it is a sound plural. Among the Arabs there are those who say *fi bid'i sinin* as they say *fi ghislin* (فِي غِسْلِينٍ). It is permissible to pluralise *sanah* (سَنَةٌ) with the sound masculine plural, with the waw and nun or the ya' and nun, because something has been deleted from it, so this plural was made a substitute for the deficiency in its singular. The original of *sanah* is *sanhah* or *sanwah*, and the sin was given a kasra in it to show that its plural lies outside its analogy and pattern. This is the view of the Basrans. Al-Farra' would be obliged to give it a damma, because he says that the damma is an indicator of the waw, and a waw has been deleted from *sanah* according to one of the two views; yet no one that we know of has given it a damma.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿To Allah belongs the command, before and after﴾. He, the Exalted, informed that He alone has the power, and that whatever victory or other matter exists in the world comes only from Him, by His will and His power. So He said: "To Allah belongs the command," meaning the execution of decrees.

"Before and after" means before this victory and after it. It was also said: before everything and after everything. *Min qablu wa-min ba'du* (مِنْ قَبْلُ وَمِنْ بَعْدُ) are two adverbs of place or time that were built on the damma, because they are defined by the deletion of what they are attached to, and they became containing what has been deleted, so they differed from the definition of nouns and resembled particles in containing [meaning]; so they were built, and they were specially given the damma because of their resemblance to the singular vocative, in that when it is made indefinite and is annexed its indeclinability ceases, and likewise these two, so they were given a damma. It is said: *min qablu wa-min ba'du*. Al-Kisa'i related from some of the Banu Asad: *lillahi al-amru min qablu wa-min ba'du*, with the first in the genitive and nunated, and the second in the damma without nunation. Al-Farra' related *min qabli wa-min ba'di* in the genitive without nunation. Al-Nahhas denied this and rejected it. Al-Farra' said in his book: "There are many things in the Qur'an whose error is evident, among them that he claimed it is permissible to say *min qabli wa-min ba'di*, whereas it is only permissible to say *min qablu wa-min ba'du* on the basis that they are indefinite." Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is "from what precedes and from what follows."

(*Wa-yawma'idhin yafrahu al-mu'minun bi-nasri Allah*) (وَيَوْمَئِذٍ يَفْرَحُ الْمُؤْمِنُونَ بِنَصْرِ اللَّهِ): this has already been mentioned.

(*Yansuru man yasha'*) (يَنْصُرُ مَنْ يَشاءُ): meaning from among His allies, because His victory is specific to the victory of His allies over their enemies. As for the victory of His enemies over His allies, that is not His victory; it is only a trial, though it may be called a triumph.

(*Wa-huwa al-'Aziz*) (وَهُوَ الْعَزِيزُ) in His retribution, (*al-Rahim*) (الرَّحِيمُ) toward those who obey Him.

**Verse 6 and 7 of Surah al-Rum (30) in al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an)**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿God's promise. God does not fail His promise﴾, because His speech is truthful.

(But most people do not know), and they are the disbelievers, and they are the majority. It is said: the intended ones are the polytheists of Makkah. The phrase (God's promise) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: He promised that promise as a promise.

Then God, may He be exalted, specified the extent of what they know, saying: "They know an outward appearance of the worldly life" (yaʿlamūna ẓāhiran mina al-ḥayāti al-dunyā), meaning the matters of their livelihood and their worldly affairs: when they sow and when they reap, and how they plant and how they build. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrimah and Qatadah. Al-Dahhak said: it is the building of its palaces, the splitting of its rivers and the planting of its trees, and the meaning is one. It is also said: it is what the devils convey to them of worldly matters when they eavesdrop from the lowest heaven; this was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr. It is also said: the outward and the inward, as He said in another place: "Or [is it] with an outward saying?" [[Qur'an 13:33. Al-Jami', vol. 9, p. 323.]]. I say: the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas is more fitting to the outward of the worldly life, so much so that al-Hasan said: By God, the knowledge of one of them about the world has reached the point that he can assess a dirham and tell you its weight, yet he does not know how to pray properly. Abu al-ʿAbbas al-Mubarrad said: Khosrow divided his days, saying: the day of wind is suited to sleep, the day of cloud to hunting, the day of rain to drinking and amusement, and the day of sun to needs. Ibn Khalawayh said: How knowledgeable they were in managing their worldly affairs, "they know an outward appearance of the worldly life."

(And they, of the Hereafter) meaning, they are heedless of knowledge of it and of working for it (they are heedless). Some of them said:

And of the calamity is that you see a companion of yours, in the form of a man who hears and sees,
Alert to every misfortune in his wealth, but when he is struck in his religion he is unaware.

"قَوْلُهُ: "فِي أَنْفُسِهِمْ"" — His saying, "fi anfusihim" (within themselves): it is a adverbial complement (zarf) of "yatafakkaru" (reflect), and not a direct object. "Yatafakkaru" is made to reach it by means of a preposition, because they were not commanded to reflect upon the creation of their own selves. Rather, they were commanded to apply reflection to the creation of the heavens and the earth and to themselves, so that they would know that Allah did not create the heavens and other than them except with truth. Al-Zajjaj said: there is an omission in the speech, meaning "fa-ya'lamu" (so that they may know), because there is an indication of it in the speech.

"(إِلَّا بِالْحَقِّ)" Al-Farra' said: its meaning is "illa lil-haqq" (except for the truth), meaning for reward and punishment. It was also said: "illa li-iqamat al-haqq" (except to establish the truth). It was also said: "bil-haqq" means "bil-'adl" (with justice). It was said: "bil-hikmah" (with wisdom), and the meanings are close. It was also said: "bil-haqq" means that He Himself is the Truth, and for the Truth He created them, and it is the indication of His Oneness and His power.

"(وَأَجَلٍ مُسَمًّى)" That is, for the heavens and the earth there is a term (ajal) at which they will end, and it is the Day of Resurrection. In this there is an alert to annihilation, and that every created thing has a term, and to the reward of the doer of good and the punishment of the doer of evil. It was also said: "wa-ajalin musamman" means He created what He created at a time He had designated for Him to create that thing in it.

"(وَإِنَّ كَثِيراً مِنَ النَّاسِ بِلِقاءِ رَبِّهِمْ لَكافِرُونَ)" The lam is for emphasis, and the estimated structure is: "la-kafiruna bi-liqa' rabbihim" (they are indeed disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord), by way of fronting and delaying, meaning they are indeed disbelievers in the resurrection after death. And you say: "inna Zaydan fi al-dar la-jalisun" (Zayd is indeed in the house, he is indeed sitting). And if you said: "inna Zaydan la-fi al-dar la-jalisun" it is permissible. But if you say: "inna Zaydan jalisun la-fi al-dar" it is not permissible, because the lam is only brought as emphasis for the subject of "inna" and its predicate, and when you bring both of them, it is not permissible to bring it. Likewise, if you say: "inna Zaydan la-jalisun la-fi al-dar" it is not permissible.

"The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and seen﴾ with their insight and their hearts."

(How was the end of those who came before them? They were stronger than these in power, and they ploughed the earth) meaning they turned it over for cultivation, because the people of Makkah were not a people of tillage. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They plough the earth﴾ [[See vol. 1, p. 453.]] [al-Baqarah: 71].

(And they built it up more than these have built it up) meaning those people built it up more than these people have built it up, yet their building did not benefit them, nor did the length of their lifespan.

(And their messengers came to them with clear proofs) meaning with miracles. It was also said: with the rulings of the law. So they disbelieved and did not believe.

(It was not Allah who wronged them) by destroying them without a sin, without messengers and without proof.

(But they were wronging themselves) through shirk and disobedience.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 30, verse 10:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then the end of those who did evil was the worst (al-su'a)﴾. Al-Su'a is on the pattern fu'la from al-su', and it is the feminine form of al-asw'a (the worst), just as al-husna is the feminine of al-ahsan (the best). It was said: what is meant here is the Fire, as Ibn 'Abbas said. The meaning of "asa'u" (they did evil) is "they associated partners (with Allah)," and this is indicated by "that they denied the signs of Allah." Al-su'a is a name of Jahannam, just as al-husna is a name of Paradise.

﴿That they denied the signs of Allah﴾: that is, because they denied, as al-Kisa'i said. It was also said: "bi-an kadhdhabu" (in that they denied). Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "thumma kana 'aqibatu alladhina" with the nominative (raf'), making "'aqibatu" the subject of kana, and it was made masculine because its feminine is not real. And "al-su'a" is the predicate of kana. The rest read it in the accusative (nasb), as the predicate of kana, and "al-su'a" in the nominative as the subject of kana. It is permissible that its subject be "al-takdhib" (the denial), so the sense becomes: "Then the denial became the end of those who did evil," and "al-su'a" would be a verbal noun (masdar) for "asa'u," or an attribute of an omitted noun, i.e., "the evil state (al-khullah al-sau'a)." It is narrated from al-A'mash that he read "thumma kana 'aqibata alladhina asa'u al-su'u" with al-su'u in the nominative. Al-Nahhas said: al-su'u is the greatest evil, and al-su'a is its feminine elative form.

﴿That they denied the signs of Allah﴾: it was said, with Muhammad and the Qur'an, as al-Kalbi said. Muqatil said: with the punishment that would descend upon them. Al-Dahhak said: with the miracles of Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿And they used to mock at them﴾.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 30, verse 11–13:

Abu 'Amr and Abu Bakr read "yurja'un" with the letter ya' (yurja'una, in the third person). The rest read it with ta' (turja'un, in the second person).

﴿And on the day the Hour is established, the criminals will be dumbfounded.﴾ Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read "yublas" with a fatha on the lam. The well-known usage in the language is: ablasa al-rajul (the man became dumbfounded) when he fell silent and his argument was cut off, and it was not expected that he would have any argument. His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿As for those who disbelieved and denied Our signs﴾ — the discussion of it has already preceded.

(And the meeting of the Hereafter) i.e., by the Resurrection (al-ba'th).

(Then they will be in the punishment, brought forth) i.e., remaining (muqimun). It has been said: gathered (majmu'un). It has been said: punished (mu'adhdhabun). It has been said: descending (nazilun), and from it is His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿When death approaches one of you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180], i.e., it descends upon him. This was said by Ibn Shajarah, and the meanings are close.

**Question 1:** Allah's words, ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾, to the end of the verse. On this there are three opinions.

The first is that it is an address to the believers, commanding them to worship and urging them to pray at these times. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The five prayers are in the Qur'an." It was asked of him: "Where?" He said: Allah the Exalted says, ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening﴾, which is the Maghrib and 'Isha' prayers; ﴿and when you enter the morning﴾, which is the Fajr prayer; ﴿and in the late afternoon﴾, which is the 'Asr prayer; ﴿and when you enter the noon﴾, which is the Zuhr prayer. This was also said by al-Dahhak and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. And from Ibn 'Abbas as well as Qatadah: the verse alludes to four prayers: the Maghrib, the Subh, the 'Asr and the Zuhr. They said: the 'Isha' al-Akhirah (the late night prayer) is in another verse, ﴿and at the approaches of the night﴾ [Hud: 114], and in mention of the times of 'awrah (the times when the body must be covered for prayer).

Al-Nahhas said: The people of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis) agree that this verse, ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾, refers to the prayers. I heard 'Ali ibn Sulayman say: "Its true meaning, in my view, is: glorify Allah in the prayers," because glorification (tasbih) occurs in the prayer.

This is the second opinion.

The third opinion is: glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. He mentioned the first opinion, but worded it as: "Pray to Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning."

As for naming the prayer "tasbih" (glorification), there are two explanations. One: because it includes the mention of tasbih in the bowing (ruku') and prostration (sujud). The second: it is derived from al-subhah (voluntary prayer), and subhah means prayer. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "They will have a subhah on the Day of Resurrection," meaning a prayer.

**Question 2:** Allah's words, ﴿And to Him is praise in the heavens and the earth﴾. This is an interjection within the speech, a praising of Him for His blessings and favours.

It was also said: the meaning of "And to Him is praise" is: the prayer is for Him, because it is distinguished by the recitation of "al-Hamd" (the Opening chapter, which begins with praise).

The first is more apparent, for praise of Allah is a kind of exalting Allah the Exalted, urging worship of Him, and seeking the continuation of His favour. So it is a different kind from prayer. And Allah knows best.

He began with the Maghrib prayer because the night precedes the day. In Surat Subhan (al-Isra'), he began with the Zuhr prayer, since it is the first prayer that Jibril (Gabriel) led the Prophet ﷺ in.

Al-Mawardi said: He specified the night prayer by the name of tasbih, and the day prayer by the name of hamd (praise), because during the day a person passes through states that require praising Allah the Exalted for them, while at night, in solitude, there is a state that requires declaring Allah free of imperfections. Therefore praise is more specific to the day, so the day prayer is named after it, and glorification is more specific to the night, so the night prayer is named after it.

**Question 3:** 'Ikrimah recited ﴿ḥīnan tumsūna wa ḥīnan tuṣbiḥūna﴾ (with "ḥīnan" in the accusative). The meaning is: "at a time when you enter the evening in it, and at a time when you enter the morning in it." The word "fīhi" (in it) has been omitted for lightness. The discussion of this is like the discussion of ﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48].

(And in the verse, "and in the evening") Al-Jawhari said: al-'Ashiyy and al-'Ashiyyah refer to the time from the Maghrib prayer until the 'Atamah (late night). You say: "I came to him in the evening of yesterday (ʿashiyyata amsi) and the evening of yesterday (ʿashiyya amsi)." The diminutive of al-'Ashiyy is 'Ushayyān, contrary to the analogy of its full form, as if they had made the diminutive of 'Ashyān, and the plural is 'Ushayyānāt. It was also said in its diminutive: 'Ushayshiyān, plural 'Ushayshiyāt. The diminutive of al-'Ashiyyah is 'Ushayshiyyah, plural 'Ushayshiyyāt. Al-'Ishā' (with a kasrah and with a madd) is like al-'Ashiyy. And al-'Ishā'ān means the Maghrib and the 'Atamah.

Some people claimed that al-'Ishā' is from the decline of the sun until the rising of dawn, and they recited:

*We rose at dawn, in the dark of night,*
*in the evening after midday had passed.*

Al-Mawardi said: The difference between al-masā' (evening) and al-'ishā' is that al-masā' is the appearance of darkness after sunset, while al-'ishā' is the end of the day as the sun inclines toward setting, and it is derived from 'asha al-'ayn (dimness of the eye), which is the lessening of light in the viewer, like the lessening of the light of the sun.
