The two meanings are close, except that the people of Madinah distinguished between them by the sequence of the speech. The sequence of the speech in the one in *al-A'raf* with damm is more fitting, since death is not from their action, and likewise bringing out. The fath in *Surat al-Rum* is more fitting to the sequence of the speech, that is: when He calls you, you come forth, that is, you obey; so the verb is more fitting. This coming forth is at the blast of Israfil, the final blast, as has passed and will come. It was also read *tukhrajun* with damm and fath on the *ta'*; al-Zamakhshari mentioned this and added nothing to it, and did not mention what we have mentioned about the distinction. And God knows best.

﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, by creation, ownership and servitude.

﴿All are obedient to Him﴾. It is narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Every *qunut* (قُنُوت) in the Qur'an is obedience." Al-Nahhas said: obedient in the manner of submission. It was also said: *qanitun* means acknowledging servitude, either by speech or by indication; this was said by 'Ikrimah, Abu Malik and al-Suddi. Ibn 'Abbas said: *qanitun* means praying. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas: "All are obedient to Him," that is, standing on the Day of Resurrection, as He said: ﴿The day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds﴾ (Al-Mutaffifin: 6), that is, for the reckoning. Al-Hasan: "All stand to Him, bearing witness that they are His servants." Sa'id ibn Jubayr: *qanitun* means sincere.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 30, verse 27:

His saying, exalted is He: (And it is He who originates creation, then repeats it). As for the beginning of His creation, it is His forming within the womb before birth; and as for its repetition, it is His giving life after death by the second blast for the Resurrection. So He made what is known of the beginning of creation a proof of what is hidden of its repetition, reasoning from the witnessed to the unseen. Then He affirmed this with His saying: "And it is easier for Him." Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Umar read: "yubdi'u al-khalq" (He originates creation), from abda'a, yubdi'u. Its evidence is His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is He who originates and repeats﴾ [al-Buruj: 13].[[See vol. 19, p. 294.]] The evidence for the reading of the common people is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿As He originated you, you will return﴾ [al-A'raf: 29].[[See vol. 7, p. 187 onward.]] "Ahwan" (easier) here means hayyin (easy), i.e., repetition is easy for Him. This was said by al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym and al-Hasan. So "ahwan" means "hayyin," because nothing is easier for God than anything else. Abu Ubayda said: whoever takes "ahwan" to express the comparison of one thing with another, his view is rejected by His saying: ﴿And that was ever easy for God﴾ [al-Nisa': 130] and by His saying: ﴿And their preservation does not burden Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255]. The Arabs use the form af'al in the sense of fa'il, and from this is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

Indeed He who raised the heaven built for us
a house whose supports are mighty and lofty

That is, its supports are mighty and tall. Another said:[[The speaker is Ma'n ibn Aws.]]

By your life, I do not know, and indeed I am fearful,
over which of us death will first come

He meant: "indeed I am fearful" (wajil). Abu Ubayda also recited:

Indeed I give you aversion, and indeed I,
by oath to you, despite the aversion, am inclined (la-amyal)

He meant "inclined" (ma'il).[[The verse is by al-Ahwas ibn Muhammad al-Ansari.]] Ahmad ibn Yahya recited:

Men wish that I die, and if I die,
that is a path in which I am not the only one (bi-awhad)

He meant "one" (wahid). Another said:

By your life, indeed al-Zibriqan is generous
with his kindness to the young, and more excellent (afdal)

That is, "and excellent" (fadil). From this is their saying: "Allahu akbar," whose meaning is "Allah the Great." Ma'mar related from Qatadah, who said: in the reading of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud it is: "wa huwa 'alayhi hayyin" (and it is easy for Him). Mujahid, Ikrimah and al-Dahhak said: the meaning is that repetition is easier for Him, that is, for God, than beginning, i.e., easier, though all of it is easy for God Exalted. Ibn Abbas also said this. Its reasoning is that this is an example God set for His servants: the repetition of a thing upon creatures is easier than its initiation; so the resurrection for the one who is able to originate, according to you and among you, should be easier for Him than creating. It was also said: the pronoun in "alayhi" refers to the created beings, i.e., it is easier for them, the creatures, who will be called with a single cry and then stand up, and it will be said to them: "Be," and they will be; that is easier for them than being drops, then clots, then lumps of flesh, then fetuses, then infants, then boys, then youths, then men or women. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Qutrub. It was also said: "ahwan" means "ashal" (easier). The poet said:

Easy for Asma' was the separation of the homeland,
though a lover yearns for her and longs (wa-lah yahinnu ilayha)

That is, it was easy for her. Al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym, regarding His saying exalted is He: "And it is easier for Him," said: nothing is difficult for God. Ikrimah said: the unbelievers marvelled at God's giving life to the dead, so this verse was revealed. "And His is the highest likeness" means: whatever He willed, occurred. Al-Khalil said: "al-mathal" means the attribute, i.e., His is the highest attribute "in the heavens and the earth," as He said: ﴿The likeness of Paradise which the righteous are promised﴾ [al-Ra'd: 35], meaning its description. The discussion of this has already passed.[[See vol. 9, p. 324.]] From Mujahid: "al-mathal al-a'la" is the saying "There is no god but Allah," and its meaning is: the one who has the highest attribute, that is, the attribute of unity. Qatadah likewise said: the highest likeness is the testimony that there is no god but Allah, and this is supported by His saying: ﴿He has coined for you a likeness from yourselves﴾, as we will explain shortly, God willing. Al-Zajjaj said: "And His is the highest likeness in the heavens and the earth," i.e., His saying "And it is easier for Him" has been set forth by Him as a likeness for you regarding what is hard and what is easy, intending the first explanation. Ibn Abbas said: meaning, there is nothing like Him. ﴿And He is the Mighty, the Wise﴾ has been mentioned before.[[See vol. 1, p. 287, and vol. 2, p. 131.]]

**Issue one:** In His words, ﴿from yourselves﴾, then He said, "from partners," then He said, "from what your right hands possess." The first ﴿min﴾ (مِنْ) is for the starting point (li-l-ibtida', "from"). It is as if He said: He took an example and drew it from the closest thing to you, which is yourselves. The second ﴿min﴾ (مِنْ) in "from partners" (مِنْ شُرَكاءَ) is partitive (lil-tab'id, "some of"). The third, in "from what your right hands possess" (مِمَّا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمانُكُمْ), is superfluous (za'idah), used to emphasise the interrogative.

The verse was revealed concerning the disbelievers of Quraysh. They used to say in the talbiyah (the pilgrim's call, "Here I am"): "Here I am, You have no partner, except a partner who belongs to You, whom You own and what he owns." This was related by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Qatadah said: This is an example (mathal) that God struck for the polytheists. The meaning is: Would any one of you be content for his slave to be his equal in his property and his person? If you are not content with this for yourselves, how then do you make partners for God?

**Issue two:** Some scholars said: This verse is a foundation (asl) for the principle of partnership among created beings, due to their mutual need of one another, and for the negation of partnership from God, glory be to Him. When He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿He has coined for you a parable from yourselves: Do you have, from among what your right hands possess, any partners in what We have provided for you?﴾, they must say: "Our slaves are not our partners in what You have provided us!" It is then said to them: How can it be conceived that you exempt yourselves from sharing with your slaves, while you make My slaves My partners in My creation? This is a corrupt judgement, shallow reasoning, and blindness of heart! Since partnership between slaves and their masters is void in what the masters own, and all creation are slaves of God, Exalted, it is impossible that anything in the world should be a partner of God in any of His acts. Nothing remains except that He is One, for whom partnership is impossible, since partnership requires mutual assistance, while we are in need of helping one another with wealth and labour, and the Eternal, the Pre-existent, is exalted above that, Mighty and Majestic.

This question is more beneficial for the seeker than memorising a complete register of jurisprudence (fiqh), because all bodily acts of worship are not valid except by the correct establishment of this matter in the heart. So understand this.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Rather, those who did wrong followed their own desires without knowledge﴾. When the proof had been established against them, He mentioned that they worship idols by following their desires in worshipping them and by blindly imitating their forefathers in that.

﴿So who can guide one whom Allah has sent astray?﴾ That is, there is no guide for one whom Allah the Exalted has sent astray. In this there is a refutation of the Qadariyya.

﴿And they have no helpers﴾

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 30, verse 30 (part 1 of 3):**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So set your face toward the religion, inclining to truth, the nature (fitrah) of Allah upon which He created mankind﴾. There are three issues concerning this.

The first: al-Zajjaj said: "*fitrata* (فِطْرَتَ) is in the accusative because it is in the sense of *ittabi'* (اتَّبِعْ), meaning: follow the nature of Allah." He said: "This is because the meaning of *fa-aqim wajhaka lil-din* (فَأَقِمْ وَجْهَكَ لِلدِّينِ) is: follow the upright religion and follow the nature of Allah." Al-Tabari said: "*Fitrata Allah* (فِطْرَتَ اللَّهِ) is a verbal noun (masdar) from the sense of *fa-aqim wajhaka*, because the meaning of that is: Allah originated (fatara) mankind upon that, as an origination (fitrah)." It has also been said: the meaning of this is "follow the religion of Allah, for which He created mankind." According to this opinion, the pause on *hanifan* (حَنِيفاً) is complete. According to the first two opinions, the sentence is continuous, so one does not pause on *hanifan*. The *fitrah* was called *din* (religion) because people are created for it. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 56]. [See vol. 17, p. 55.] It is said that *'alayha* (عَلَيْهَا) means *lahā* (لَهَا), as in His saying: ﴿And if you do evil, it is for yourselves﴾ [Al-Isra: 7]. [See vol. 10, p. 217.]

The address in *aqim wajhaka* (أَقِمْ وَجْهَكَ) is to the Prophet (ﷺ), commanding him to set his face toward the straight religion, as He said: ﴿So set your face toward the upright religion﴾ [Ar-Rum: 43]. [See p. 42 of this volume.] This religion is Islam. *Iqamat al-wajh* (إِقَامَةُ الْوَجْهِ) means straightening one's intention and being determined in earnestness in the acts of religion. The face was singled out for mention because it gathers the senses of a person and is the most noble of them. By scholarly consensus among the people of ta'wil (interpretation), his community is also included in this address. *Hanif* (حَنِيفاً) means upright, turning away from all the distorted and abrogated (naskh, i.e. abrogated by later revelation) religions.

The second: It is authentically narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No child is born except upon the *fitrah*" — in another narration: "upon this creed" — "and his parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian, just as an animal gives birth to a complete animal. Do you see any mutilation in it?" Then Abu Hurayrah said: Recite if you wish: "The nature of Allah upon which He created mankind; there is no altering of the creation of Allah." In another narration: "until you are the ones who slit its ears." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, what about one who dies young?" He said: "Allah knows best what they would have done." This is the wording of Muslim.

The third: Scholars differed over the meaning of *al-fitrah* mentioned in the Book and the Sunnah, giving several opinions. Among them: it is Islam. This was said by Abu Hurayrah, Ibn Shihab (al-Zuhri), and others. They said: this is the well-known view among the majority of the early scholars (salaf) of ta'wil. They argued with the verse and the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, and they reinforced this with the hadith of Iyad ibn Himar al-Mujashi'i, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to the people one day: "Shall I not tell you what Allah has told me in His Book? Allah created Adam and his descendants as *hunafa'* (upright ones) and Muslims, and gave them wealth lawful, with nothing unlawful in it, but they made lawful and unlawful from what Allah had given them..." (the hadith). And with his saying (ﷺ): "Five are of the *fitrah*..." — and he mentioned among them trimming the moustache, which is among the *sunan* (recommended practices) of Islam. According to this interpretation, the meaning of the hadith is that the child is created free from disbelief, upon the covenant which Allah took from the descendants of Adam when He brought them forth from his loins; and that if they die before reaching maturity, they are in Paradise, whether they are children of Muslims or children of disbelievers.

Others said: *al-fitrah* is the *bada'ah* (beginning) upon which Allah originated them, that is, upon what Allah created His creation with, that He originated them for life and death, happiness and misery, and for what they will become at maturity. They said: *al-fitrah* in the speech of the Arabs means the beginning, and *al-fatir* (الْفَاطِرُ) means the originator. They argued with what is reported from Ibn Abbas, that he said: "I did not know what *Fatir* of the heavens and the earth meant until two Bedouins came disputing over a well, and one of them said: 'I *fatartuha*' (أَنَا فَطَرْتُهَا), meaning: I began it." Al-Marwazi said: Ahmad ibn Hanbal used to hold this view, then he abandoned it. Abu Umar (Ibn Abd al-Barr) said in his book *al-Tamhid*: what Malik recorded in his *Muwatta'* and what he mentioned in the chapter on *qadar* (divine decree) of the reports in it indicates that his view on this matter is similar to this, and Allah knows best.

Among what they argued with is what is reported from Ka'b al-Qurazi concerning the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿A group He guided, and a group upon whom misguidance was deserved﴾ [Al-A'raf: 30]. [See vol. 7, p. 188 onward.] He said: Whomever Allah originated for misguidance, He will make him end in misguidance even if he does the deeds of guidance; and whomever Allah originated upon guidance, He will make him end in guidance even if he does the deeds of misguidance. Allah originated the creation of Iblis upon misguidance, and he did the deeds of happiness with the angels, then Allah returned him to what He had originated His creation upon. He said: "And he was among the disbelievers."

I say: The saying of Ka'b has already passed in *al-A'raf*, and its meaning has come in a raised (marfu') report from the hadith of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was called to the funeral of a young boy from the Ansar. I said: "O Messenger of Allah, how fortunate is this, a little bird from the little birds of Paradise, who did no evil and did not reach it!" He said: "Or other than that, O Aisha! Allah created for Paradise people whom He created for it while they were in their fathers' loins, and He created for the Fire people whom He created for it while they were in their fathers' loins." Ibn Majah recorded it in *al-Sunan*.

Abu Isa al-Tirmidhi also narrated from Abdullah ibn Amr, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came out to us with two books in his hand, and he said: "Do you know what these two books are?" We said: "No, O Messenger of Allah, unless you inform us." He said to the one in his right hand: "This is a book from the Lord of the worlds, containing the names of the people of Paradise, the names of their fathers and their tribes, then the total is summed up at the end of them, so nothing will be added to them and nothing will be subtracted from them, ever." Then he said to the one in his left hand: "This is a book from the Lord of the worlds, containing the names of the people of the Fire and the names of their fathers and their tribes, then the total is summed up at the end of them, so nothing will be added to them and nothing will be subtracted from them, ever..."

(He mentioned the hadith and said of it: "It is a good (hasan) hadith.") A group said: The intended meaning of His words, Exalted is He, "the nature (fitrah) on which He created mankind" [Ar-Rum 30:30], and of the words of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Every child is born upon the fitrah" [Bukhari and Muslim], is not generality. Rather, by "mankind" is meant the believers, since if all were created upon Islam, none would disbelieve. It is established that He created groups for the Fire, as He said: ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind﴾ [Al-A'raf 7:179]. [See vol. 7, p. 324.] [Al-A'raf: ﴿And He brought forth from the loins of Adam their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves﴾, and (the text reads) black and white.] He also said, concerning the boy whom al-Khidr killed: "He was sealed on the day he was sealed as a disbeliever." Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led us in the afternoon (asr) prayer while it was still daytime [meaning the sun was high], and in it he said, among what we memorized: "Behold, the children of Adam were created in diverse classes. Some of them are born believers, live as believers and die as believers; some are born disbelievers, live as disbelievers and die as disbelievers; some are born believers, live as believers and die as disbelievers; some are born disbelievers, live as disbelievers and die as believers; and among them is the one of good judgment and good seeking." Hammad ibn Zayd ibn Salama [the word "Maslama" is omitted in manuscripts J and Sh] mentioned it in the Musnad of al-Tayalisi, saying: Ali ibn Zayd narrated to us from Abu Nadra from Abu Sa'id.

They said: Generality in the sense of particularity is common in the Arabic language. Do you not see the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿destroying everything by the command of its Lord﴾, yet nothing was seen except their dwellings; and they did not destroy the heavens and the earth [Al-Ahqaf 46:25; see vol. 16, p. 205]. And His words: ﴿We opened upon them the gates of everything﴾ [Al-An'am 6:44; see vol. 6, p. 425], yet the gates of mercy were not opened to them.

Ishaq ibn Rahawayh al-Hanzali said: The speech is complete at His words: ﴿So set your face toward the religion, inclining to truth﴾ [Ar-Rum 30:30]. Then (it continues): ﴿the fitrah of Allah﴾, meaning Allah originated creation with a fitrah, either toward Paradise or toward the Fire. The Prophet (ﷺ) alluded to this in his words: "Every child is born upon the fitrah." For this reason He said: ﴿There is no alteration in the creation of Allah﴾ [Ar-Rum 30:30].

Our shaykh Abu al-Abbas said: Whoever says it is the precedence of happiness and wretchedness, this fits the fitrah mentioned in the Qur'an, because Allah, Exalted is He, said: "There is no alteration in the creation of Allah." But as for the hadith, no, because it has informed in the rest of the hadith that it is changed and altered.

A group of the people of jurisprudence and reasoning said: The fitrah is the creation upon which the child is made, in knowledge of its Lord. It is as if he said: Every child is born upon a creation by which he knows his Lord when he reaches the stage of knowledge, meaning a creation different from the creation of the beasts, which do not, through their creation, arrive at knowledge of Him.

They argued that fitrah means creation and al-fatir means the Creator, from the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Praise be to Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Fatir 35:1; see vol. 14, p. 318 ff.], meaning their Creator; and by His words: ﴿And what is wrong with me that I should not worship Him who originated me?﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:22; see vol. 15, p. 17], meaning who created me; and by His words: ﴿He who originated them﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 21:56; see vol. 11, p. 296], meaning who created them. They said: So fitrah is creation and al-fatir is the Creator. They denied that the child is originated upon disbelief, faith, knowledge or denial. They said: Rather, the child is upon soundness, for the most part, in creation, nature and constitution, with no faith, disbelief, denial or knowledge accompanying it. Then they come to believe in disbelief or faith after puberty, when they discern.

They argued by his words in the hadith: "Just as a beast gives birth to a complete beast; do you perceive in it any mutilation?" meaning cut ears. Thus he likened the hearts of the children of Adam to beasts, because they are born with complete creation, without deficiency; then their ears and noses are afterward cut, and it is said: "This is a bahira and this is a sa'iba" [see vol. 6, p. 335]. He says: Likewise the hearts of children at the time of their birth have neither disbelief nor faith, neither knowledge nor denial, like grazing beasts. When they reach maturity, the devils lead them astray, so most of them disbelieve, and Allah protects the few.

They said: If children were originated upon some disbelief or faith at the beginning of their affairs, they would never leave it, yet we find them believing and then disbelieving. They said: It is impossible in reason that the child at the time of birth understands disbelief or faith, because Allah brought them forth in a state in which they understand nothing. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah brought you forth from the wombs of your mothers, knowing nothing﴾ [An-Nahl 16:78; see vol. 10, p. 151]. Thus whoever knows nothing cannot have disbelief, faith, knowledge or denial. Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: This is the most sound of what has been said about the meaning of the fitrah upon which people are born. Among the proofs for this also is the words of the Exalted: ﴿You shall only be recompensed for what you used to do﴾ [At-Tur 52:16; see vol. 17, p. 62 ff.], and ﴿every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned﴾ [Al-Muddaththir 74:38; see vol. 19, p. 82 ff.]. Whoever has not reached the time of action is not held in pledge for anything. And He said: ﴿And We would not punish until We sent a messenger﴾ [Al-Isra' 17:15; see vol. 10, p. 231 ff.]. Since they agreed to remove retaliation (qawad), retribution (qisas), the prescribed punishments (hudud) and sins from them in the life of this world, the Hereafter is more deserving of this. And Allah knows best.

It is impossible that the fitrah mentioned be Islam, as Ibn Shihab (al-Zuhri) said, because Islam and faith are: speech with the tongue, belief in the heart, and action with the limbs. This is absent in the child, and no person of intellect is ignorant of that.

As for the words of al-Awza'i: I asked al-Zuhri about a man who owed a slave to be freed: is it sufficient for him to free a child who is still nursing? He said: Yes, because he was born upon the fitrah, meaning Islam. The freeing is valid according to whoever permits it, because his ruling is the ruling of his parents. Others disagreed with them and said: In obligatory emancipations, only one who fasts and prays is acceptable. And in His words: ﴿As He originated you, so you will return﴾ [Al-A'raf 7:29; see vol. 7, p. 187 ff.], and in (the saying): "that Allah may seal for the servant with what He decreed for him and destined upon him," there is no evidence that the child is born at the time of birth as a believer or a disbeliever, since the intellects testify that at that time he is not one who understands faith or disbelief. The hadith in which it came: "Indeed, the people were created in classes" is not among the hadiths free from criticism, because Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an transmitted it alone, and Shu'ba [the word "Shu'ba" is omitted in manuscript J] used to speak about him. Furthermore, his words "he is born a believer" may mean: he is born in order to be a believer, and he is born in order to be a disbeliever according to Allah's prior knowledge concerning him. And in his words in the hadith ("I created these for Paradise and I created these for the Fire") there is nothing more than regard for what they will be sealed with, not that they, in their childhood, are among those who deserve Paradise or Fire, or understand disbelief or faith.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 30, verse 30 (part 3 of 3):

I say: Among those who adopted the view that Abu 'Umar (Ibn 'Abd al-Barr) preferred and argued for are a number of the verifying scholars (al-muhaqqiqin), including Ibn 'Atiyyah in his tafsir regarding the meaning of al-fitrah, and our shaykh Abu al-'Abbas. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "What is relied upon in explaining this term is that it is the creation and the disposition that is in the nature of the child, which is prepared and made ready so that by it he may distinguish the creatures of God, be guided by them to his Lord, know His laws, and believe in Him. It is as if God, exalted is He, said: Set your face toward the religion that is upright (al-hanif), and it is the fitrah of God upon which He created mankind, prepared for it. But circumstances befall them. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: (Every child is born upon the fitrah; then his parents make him a Jew or a Christian)." Mention of the two parents is merely an example of the many circumstances that occur.

Our shaykh said in his expression: God, exalted is He, created the hearts of the children of Adam fit to accept the truth, just as He created their eyes and ears capable of perceiving visible and audible things. So long as they remain upon that acceptance and that capacity, they attain the truth and the religion of Islam, which is the true religion. The saying of the Prophet ﷺ confirms the soundness of this meaning: (Just as an animal gives birth to a complete animal; do you see in it any mutilation?) That is, the animal bears its young in complete form, sound from defects. If it were left upon the original form of that creation, it would remain complete and free from flaws, but it is altered, its ear is cut and its face branded, so afflictions and defects befall it and it departs from its original state. Likewise is the human being. This is an apt comparison, and its aspect is clear.

I say: This view, together with the first view, agrees with it in meaning, and that [the covenant] is after attaining understanding, when they comprehend the affairs of this world, and God's proof against them is confirmed by the manifest signs He set up: the creation of the heavens and the earth, the sun and the moon, the land and the sea, and the alternation of night and day. When their desires worked upon them, the devils came to them and called them to Judaism and Christianity, and so their desires carried them to the right and the left. As for those who die young, they are in Paradise, I mean all children, because when God, exalted is He, brought forth the offspring of Adam from his loins in the form of atoms, they acknowledged Him as Lord, as is His saying, exalted is He: "And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their offspring [[Recitation of Nafi', and with it the author used to recite.]] and made them testify concerning themselves: 'Am I not your Lord?' They said: 'Yes, we testify'" [[See vol. 7, p. 314 and following.]] [al-A'raf: 172]. Then He returned them to the loins of Adam after they had acknowledged Him as Lord and that He is God, there is no god but Him. Then the servant is recorded in his mother's womb as wretched or happy, according to the first Book. Whoever is recorded in the first Book as wretched is allowed to live until the pen runs over him, and so he breaks the covenant that was taken from him in the loins of Adam by associating partners with Him. Whoever is recorded in the first Book as happy is allowed to live until the pen runs over him, and so he becomes happy. Whoever of the children of the Muslims dies young before the pen runs over him is with his fathers in Paradise. Whoever is of the children of the polytheists and dies before the pen runs over him, they are not with their fathers, because they died upon the first covenant that was taken from them in the loins of Adam, and did not break the covenant. This was held by a group of the interpreters, and it reconciles the hadiths. The meaning of his saying, peace be upon him, when he was asked about the children of the polytheists, and he said: (God knows best what they would have done), is: had they reached maturity. This interpretation is also supported by the hadith of al-Bukhari from Samurah ibn Jundub from the Prophet ﷺ, the long hadith of the dream, in which he, peace be upon him, said: (As for the tall man in the garden, he is Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and as for the children around him, every child born upon the fitrah.) He said: It was said: "O Messenger of God, and the children of the polytheists?" The Messenger of God ﷺ said: (And the children of the polytheists.) This is a text that removes the disagreement, and it is the soundest thing narrated on this subject. Other hadiths on it have defects and are not among the hadiths of the leading jurists, as said by Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr. It has been narrated from the hadith of Anas, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ was asked about the children of the polytheists, and he said: (They had no good deeds for which they would be rewarded, so that they would be among the kings of Paradise, and they had no evil deeds for which they would be punished, so that they would be among the people of the Fire; they are servants to the people of Paradise.) Yahya ibn Salam mentioned it in his tafsir. We have added more explanation of this question in our book al-Tadhkirah, and we mentioned in our book al-Muqtabas fi Sharh Muwatta' Malik ibn Anas what Abu 'Umar mentioned on this, and praise be to God. Ishaq ibn Rahawayh mentioned, saying: Yahya ibn Adam told us, saying: Jarir ibn Hazim informed us, from Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi, who said: I heard Ibn 'Abbas say: The affair of this nation will not cease to be smooth or close, or a word resembling these two, until they speak or look into the matter of children and destiny. Yahya ibn Adam said: I mentioned this to Ibn al-Mubarak, and he said: Does a person remain silent upon ignorance? I said: So do you order speech? He said: So he fell silent. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: "The fitrah of God upon which He created mankind" is poverty and neediness, and this is good, for from the time he is born until he dies he is poor and in need, yes! And in the Hereafter.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is no altering of the creation of God﴾, that is, this fitrah has no alteration from the side of the Creator, and the matter cannot come contrary to this in any way; that is, whoever He created happy will not be wretched, and whoever He created wretched will not be happy. Mujahid said: the meaning is: there is no changing of the religion of God. Qatadah, Ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd and al-Nakha'i said the same, saying: this is its meaning regarding beliefs. 'Ikrimah said: It has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that the meaning is: there is no changing of God's creation among the animals by castrating their males; so its meaning is the prohibition of castrating male animals. This has passed in "al-Nisa'" [[See vol. 5, p. 389 and following.]]. And that is ﴿the upright religion﴾, that is, that correct judgment, said by Ibn 'Abbas. Muqatil said: that is the clear reckoning. It was also said: "That is the upright religion," that is, the religion of Islam is the upright, straight religion.
﴿But most people do not know﴾, that is, they do not reflect so that they would know that they have a Creator who is worshipped, and a eternal God whose decree preceded and whose command took effect.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 30, verse 31–32:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿turning back to Him in repentance﴾ — its meaning has been disputed. It was said: returning to Him in repentance and sincerity. Yahya ibn Sallam and al-Farra' said: turning towards Him. Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: obedient to Him. And it was said: repenting to Him from sins [[The phrase "from sins" (من الذنوب) is omitted in manuscript ج.]], and from this is the verse of Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat:

"So if they repent, then Banu Sulaym ... and their people Hawazin have indeed turned back in repentance."

The meaning is one, for "nāba, tāba, thāba and āba" all mean return. Al-Mawardi said: Regarding the original sense of inabah (turning in devotion) there are two opinions. The first: its origin is cutting, and from it is taken the name of the nāb (fang/canine tooth), because it cuts; so inabah is the severing of oneself to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, through obedience. The second: its origin is return, taken from nāba yanūbu when one returns again and again, and from it comes nawbah (a turn), because it is a return to a habit. Al-Jawhari said: "And anāba ilā Allāh" means "aqbala wa tāba" (he turned towards Allah and repented). The nawbah is the singular of nawab (turns); you say: "your turn has come" (jā'at nawbatuka wa-niyābatuka), and they take turns (yatanāwabūn al-nawbah) among themselves in water and other things.

It is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Muhammad ibn Yazid said: because the meaning of "Set your face" is "so set your faces, turning back in repentance." Al-Farra' said: the meaning is "so set your face, and those with you, turning back in repentance." It was also said: it is in the accusative by way of detachment (qaṭ'), meaning: "so set your face, you and your community, turning back in repentance to Him," because the command addressed to him is a command to his community; therefore it is fitting to say "turning back in repentance to Him." Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾ [al-Talaq: 1] [[See vol. 18, p. 147.]].

(And fear Him) i.e., be mindful of Him and carry out what He has commanded you.

(And establish the prayer and do not be among the polytheists [He made clear that worship benefits only with sincerity, therefore He said: "and do not be among the polytheists" [[What is between the brackets is omitted in manuscript ج.]]]) This has already been explained in detail "in al-Nisa' and al-Kahf" [[See vol. 5, p. 180 and vol. 11, p. 96.]] and elsewhere.

(Of those who divided their religion) Abu Hurayrah, Aishah and Abu Umamah interpreted it as referring to the people of the qiblah among the followers of desires and innovations. Its explanation has already passed "in al-An'am" [[See vol. 7, p. 149 and p. 240.]]. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: those who divided their religion are the People of the Book, the Jews and the Christians, and Qatadah and Ma'mar said the same. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read: "fāraqū dīnahum" (they separated from their religion), and Ali ibn Abi Talib also read it thus, meaning: they departed from their religion which must be followed, namely monotheism (tawhid).

(And became sects) i.e., factions, as said by al-Kalbi. It was also said: religions, as said by Muqatil.

(Each faction rejoicing in what they have) i.e., pleased and self-satisfied, because they have not clarified the truth, whereas it is incumbent upon them to clarify it. It was also said: this was before the obligations were revealed. A third view: one who disobeys Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, may rejoice in his disobedience; likewise Satan, highway robbers and others. And Allah knows best. Al-Farra' claimed that it is permissible for the sentence to end at "and do not be among the polytheists," and the meaning would be: "of those who separated from their religion," and "and became sects" would be a new sentence; and that it is also permissible for it to be connected to what precedes it. [Al-Nahhas: When it is connected to what precedes it,] it is, according to the Basrans, in apposition (badal) with the repetition of the preposition, as the Exalted said: ﴿The eminent ones of his people who were arrogant said to those who were oppressed, to those of them who believed﴾ [al-A'raf: 75]; and had it been without the preposition, it would have been permissible.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 30, verse 33:

The words of the Most High: ﴿And when harm touches mankind﴾, i.e., drought and hardship, (they call upon their Lord) to remove it from them (turning back to Him in repentance). Ibn 'Abbas said: turning toward Him with their whole hearts, not associating (anything with Him).

The meaning of this statement is one of wonder. His Prophet marvelled at the polytheists for abandoning turning back (inabah) to God, the Most High, despite the successive proofs against them. That is: when harm, from sickness or hardship, touches these disbelievers, they call upon their Lord, i.e., they seek His help to remove what has befallen them, turning to Him alone and not to the idols, because they know that there is no relief with them.

(Then when He gives them a taste of mercy from Him) i.e., well-being and blessing.

(Behold, a group of them associate others with their Lord) i.e., they associate others with Him in worship.

"The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿so that they may disbelieve in what We have given them﴾. It has been said: it is the lam of purpose (lam kay). And it has been said: it is a lam of command carrying the meaning of threat, as the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ [al-Kahf: 29].[[See vol. 10, p. 392 and onward.]]

(So enjoy yourselves, for you will soon know.) This is a threat and a warning. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud it reads "wa-liyatamatta'u" (and let them enjoy themselves), meaning: We enabled them to do so in order that they might enjoy themselves. It is then a report about an absent party, like "liyakfuru" (so that they may disbelieve). And according to the script of the codex, it is an address after a report about an absent party, meaning: enjoy yourselves, you who act upon this."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 30, verse 35:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or have We sent down to them an authority (sultan)?﴾ It is an interrogative with the sense of reproach (tawqif). Al-Dahhak said: "sultan" means a book. Qatadah and al-Rabi' ibn Anas also said this. The speech was attributed to the book figuratively (tawassu'an). Al-Farra' claimed that the Arabs make sultan feminine, saying: "The sultan has judged against you in this matter" (qadat bihi 'alayka al-sultanu). As for the Basrians, the masculine is more eloquent in their view, and the Quran came with it, while the feminine is permissible in their view because it means proof (hujjah), i.e., a proof that speaks of your polytheism. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and also by al-Dahhak. 'Ali ibn Sulayman related from Abu al-'Abbas Muhammad ibn Yazid, who said: sultan is a plural of salit, like raghif and raghfan, so its masculine form is according to the sense of plurality and its feminine form according to the sense of group (jama'ah). The discussion of sultan has already been covered fully in (Al 'Imran) [[See vol. 4, p. 233.]]. And sultan is that by which a person defends himself against a matter that would entail punishment, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Or I will surely slaughter him, or he must bring me a clear authority﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 176 and what follows.]] [al-Naml: 21].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 30, verse 36:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when We let people taste mercy, they rejoice in it﴾, meaning fertility, abundance and well-being. This was said by Yahya ibn Sallam. Al-Naqqash said: it means blessing and rain. It was also said: security and ease. The meanings are close to one another. "They rejoice in it" means in the mercy.

(And if an evil befalls them) meaning a trial and a punishment. This was said by Mujahid. Al-Suddi said: a drought of rain.

(Because of what their hands have sent forward) meaning because of what they have done of acts of disobedience.

(Then they despair) meaning they lose hope of mercy and relief [[In manuscripts K and Sh: (al-farah) with a ḥ.]]. This was said by the majority of scholars. Al-Hasan said: despair is abandoning the obligations of Allah, may He be glorified and exalted, in secret. The verb is qanita yaqnatu, and this is the reading of the common readers. Qanata yaqnitu is the reading of Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub. Al-A'mash recited "qanita yaqnitu" (Al-Hijr: 56) with kasra in both places, like hasiba yahsibu. The verse describes the disbeliever, who despairs at hardship and becomes insolent at blessing, as it has been said:

Like a bad donkey: if you feed it, it kicks people; and if it is hungry, it brays.

Many who have not had faith firmly settled in their hearts are of this condition, and this has passed in more than one place. As for the believer, he gives thanks to his Lord at blessing and hopes in Him at hardship.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 30, verse 37:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they not see that Allah extends provision for whom He wills and restricts it?﴾ That is, He widens goodness in this world for whomever He wills, or restricts it, so poverty should not drive them to despair.

(Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe.)

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 30, verse 38:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So give to the near of kin his right﴾. In this there are three issues.

The first: since it was previously stated that He, glory be to Him, expands provision for whomever He wills [[The text between the two brackets is omitted from manuscript K.]] and restricts it, He commanded the one to whom He has extended provision to deliver to the poor what suffices him, in order to test the gratitude of the wealthy. The address is to the Prophet, peace be upon him, and what is meant is he and his community, because He said: ﴿That is better for those who desire the Face of Allah﴾. He commanded giving to the near of kin because of the closeness of their kinship, and the best charity is that which is given to a relative, and in it is the maintaining of ties of kinship (silat al-rahim). The Messenger of Allah ﷺ preferred charity given to relatives over freeing slaves. He said to Maymunah, when she had freed a slave girl: "As for you, if you had given her to your maternal uncles, it would have been greater for your reward."

The second: this verse has been disputed. It was said that it is abrogated by the verse of inheritance. It was also said: there is no abrogation, rather the relative has a binding right in righteousness in every circumstance, and this is the sound view. Mujahid and Qatadah said: maintaining ties of kinship is an obligation from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to the point that Mujahid said: no charity from anyone is accepted while his relative is in need. It was also said: what is meant by "the near of kin" is the relatives of the Prophet ﷺ. The first view is more correct, for their right is specified in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in His saying: ﴿And know that whatever you obtain of war booty, a fifth of it is for Allah and for the Messenger and for the near of kin﴾ [al-Anfal: 41]. It was also said that the command to give to the near of kin is by way of recommendation (nadb). Al-Hasan said: "its right" is consoling in ease, and a kind word in hardship.

﴿And the needy﴾: Ibn Abbas said: that is, feed the one who asks and goes around, and the wayfarer: the guest, thus he made hospitality an obligation. All of this has been explained at length and clarified in its appropriate places, and praise be to Allah.

The third: ﴿That is better for those who desire the Face of Allah﴾, meaning: giving the right is better than withholding when it is intended by that the Face of Allah and drawing near to Him.

﴿And those are the successful ones﴾, meaning: those who attain their sought reward in the Hereafter. The discussion of this has already preceded in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 181.]].

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 30, verse 39:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whatever you give as riba (an increase, here meaning a gift given for a return) so that it may increase within people's wealth, it does not increase with God﴾. On this verse there are four issues.

The first: When He mentioned what is intended for His countenance and what persists upon it, He mentioned other than that from the attribute, and also what is intended for His countenance. The majority of readers recited "ātaytum" with a long vowel (madd), meaning "you gave." Ibn Kathir, Mujahid and Humayd recited it without the long vowel, meaning "what you did of riba so that it may increase," as you say, "I did a correct thing (ātaytu ṣawāban)" and "I did an error (ātaytu khaṭa'an)." They agreed on the long vowel in His saying: ﴿And whatever you give as zakah﴾. Riba means increase, and its meaning has already passed in al-Baqarah (see vol. 3, p. 348 onward). There it is forbidden, and here it is permitted. By this it is established that it is of two kinds: some of it is lawful and some of it is unlawful.

Ikrimah said regarding His saying, ﴿And whatever you give as riba so that it may increase within people's wealth﴾: "Riba is of two kinds: lawful riba and unlawful riba. As for lawful riba, it is the gift that is given, seeking something better than it in return." On the authority of al-Dahhak regarding this verse: it is the lawful riba which is given as a gift so that something better may be returned for it, neither for him nor against him; there is no reward for him in it, and no sin upon him for it. Likewise Ibn Abbas said: "And whatever you give as riba" means the gift a man gives of a thing, hoping to receive something better than it. That is what does not increase with God, and its giver is not rewarded, but there is no sin upon him. In this sense the verse was revealed. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Tawus and Mujahid said: this verse was revealed concerning the gift of reward (hibat al-thawab, a gift given in expectation of a return). Ibn Atiyyah said: whatever is similar to it, which a person does in order to be repaid, such as greeting and the like, although there is no sin in it, there is no reward in it and no increase with God the Exalted. The Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi also said this.

In the Sunan of al-Nasa'i, on the authority of Abd al-Rahman ibn Alqamah, who said: The delegation of Thaqif came to the Messenger of God ﷺ, and with them was a gift. He said: (Is it a gift or a charity? If it is a gift, then it is sought for the countenance of the Messenger of God ﷺ and the fulfilment of a need; and if it is a charity, then it is sought for the countenance of God, mighty and majestic.) They said: "No, rather it is a gift." So he accepted it from them and sat with them, questioning them and they questioning him.

Ibn Abbas also said, and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i: It was revealed concerning people who give to their relatives and brothers for the sake of benefiting them, enriching them and showing favour to them, and so that they may increase their wealth by way of benefit to them. Al-Sha'bi said: the meaning of the verse is that whatever a person serves someone with and makes himself light for him in order that he may benefit from it in his worldly life, that benefit which he repays the service with does not increase with God. It was said: this was forbidden to the Prophet ﷺ specifically. God the Exalted said: ﴿And do not give in order to receive more﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 6], so He forbade him to give something and take more than it as a return. It was also said: it is the forbidden riba. According to this view, the meaning of "it does not increase with God" is that it is not counted for the one who takes it, but rather it belongs to the one from whom it was taken. Al-Suddi said: this verse was revealed concerning the riba of Thaqif, because they used to practise riba and Quraysh used to practise it upon them.

The second issue: Al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi said: the explicit meaning of the verse concerns one who gives a gift seeking an increase from people's wealth in return. Al-Muhallab said: The scholars differed concerning one who gives a gift seeking its reward and says: "I only intended the reward." Malik said: it is to be examined. If the giver is of the kind who seeks reward from the recipient, then he has that right, such as the gift of the poor to the rich, the gift of a servant to his master, or the gift of a man to his ruler or one above him. This is one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifah said: he has no reward if he did not stipulate it, and this is al-Shafi'i's other opinion. He said: a gift given for reward is void and does not benefit him, because it is a sale for an unknown price. The Kufan scholar argued that the subject of a gift is voluntary giving; if we required a return in it, the meaning of voluntary giving would be nullified and it would become like exchange contracts. The Arabs have distinguished between the word "sale" and the word "gift," making the word "sale" apply to what entitles one to a return, while the gift is otherwise.

Our evidence is what Malik related in his Muwatta' on the authority of Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "Whoever gives a gift, considering it to be for reward, then he has the right over his gift until he is satisfied from it." Similar was reported from Ali, may God be pleased with him, who said: "Gifts are of three kinds: a gift intended for the countenance of God, a gift intended for the faces of people, and a gift intended for reward. The gift for reward, its giver may take it back if he is not rewarded from it."

Al-Bukhari, may God have mercy on him, titled a chapter "The Chapter on Reciprocation in Gifts," and related the hadith of Aishah, who said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ used to accept gifts and reciprocate for them, and he reciprocated for a she-camel milk-giver (liqhah, a milch camel; the word is pronounced with either vowel on the lam, meaning a milch camel). He did not object to its owner when he sought reward; rather, he objected only to his displeasure at the reward, which exceeded the value." It was narrated by al-Tirmidhi.

The third issue: What Ali, may God be pleased with him, mentioned and detailed concerning gifts is correct. The giver, in his gift, is in one of three states. The first: he intends by it the countenance of God the Exalted and seeks reward from Him. The second: he intends by it the faces of people, showing off, so that they praise him for it and commend him because of it. The third: he intends by it reward from the recipient, and the discussion of this has already passed. The Prophet ﷺ said: (Actions are by intentions, and for every person is only what he intended.) As for when he intends by his gift the countenance of God the Exalted and seeks reward from Him, then he has that with God through His bounty and mercy. God, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And whatever you give as zakah seeking the countenance of God—those are the ones who receive multiplication﴾. Likewise, one who keeps ties with his relatives so that he may become wealthy and not be a burden, the intention in that is decisive. If it is to display worldly status by it, then it is not for the countenance of God; and if it is for what he is owed of the right of kinship and the bond of kinship between them, then it is for the countenance of God. As for one who intends by his gift the faces of people, showing off, so that they praise him for it and commend him because of it, there is no benefit for him in his gift: no reward in this world and no recompense in the Hereafter. God mighty and majestic said: ﴿O you who have believed, do not nullify your charities with reminders and injury, like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 264], to the end of the verse. As for one who intends by his gift the reward from the recipient, he has what he intended by his gift, and he may take it back, as long as he has not been compensated with its value, according to the school of Ibn al-Qasim; or as long as he has not been satisfied from it with more than its value, according to the apparent position of Umar and Ali. This is the view of Mutarrif in al-Wadihah: that the gift, as long as it remains in its original form, whether it has increased or decreased, the donor may take it back even if the recipient has compensated him with more than it. It has also been said: if it remains in its original form and has not changed, then he takes whatever he wishes. It has also been said: he is bound to its value, like a marriage contract without a fixed dowry. As for when the gift has been lost, he has only its value by agreement, as Ibn al-Arabi said.

The fourth issue: His saying, may He be exalted: (li-yarbū, "that it may increase"). The majority of the seven readers recited (li-yarbū) with the yā' (third person), attributing the verb to riba. Nafi' alone recited it with a ḍamma on the tā' [and the wāw] being sukūn, in the second person, meaning "that you may become those with increases." This is the recitation of Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Sha'bi. Abu Hatim said: this is our recitation. Abu Malik recited (li-turabbūhā), with a feminine pronoun.

(Fa-lā yarbū 'inda Allāh) means: it does not grow or get reward for it, because He accepts only what is intended for His countenance and is purely for Him. This has already been discussed in (al-Nisa') (see vol. 5, p. 410).

(Wa-mā ātaytum min zakāh) Ibn Abbas said: that is, of charity.

(Turīdūna wajha Allāh fa-ulā'ika hum al-mudʿifūn) meaning: that is what He accepts and multiplies for him ten times or more, as He said: ﴿Who is it that would lend to God a goodly loan so that He may multiply it for him many times over?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 245]. And He said: ﴿And the example of those who spend their wealth seeking the approval of God and strengthening of their souls is like a garden on a height﴾ [al-Baqarah: 265]. He said: "fa-ulā'ika hum al-mudʿifūn" and did not say "fa-antum al-mudʿifūn," because He shifted from address (the second person) to the third person, like His saying: ﴿Until when you are in the ships and they sail with them﴾ [Yunus: 22]. Regarding the meaning of al-mudʿifīn there are two opinions. The first: their good deeds are multiplied for them, as we have mentioned. The second: good and blessing are multiplied for them, that is, they are people of multiples, as one says: "So-and-so is muqwin" when his camels are strong; and "musmin" when his camels are fat; and "mu'tash" when his camels are thirsty; and "mud'if" when his camels are weak. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: (O God, I seek refuge in You from the wicked, the one who makes wicked, Satan the accursed). So "al-mukhbith" is one who has been afflicted with corruption (khubth). It is said: "So-and-so is radī'," meaning he is inferior in himself; and "mardi'," meaning those with him are inferior (ird'ā'). *(end)*

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 30, verse 40:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is Allah who created you﴾. It is an inchoative (ibtida') and a predicate (khabar). The discourse returns to arguing against the polytheists, that He is the Creator, the Provider, the One who causes death and gives life. Then He said, in the form of a question: ﴿Is there any of your partners who does anything of that?﴾

No, none does. Then He declared Himself free of rivals (andad), opposites (adrad), consorts (sahiba) and offspring (awlad) by His true saying: ﴿Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾ He attributed the "partners" to them because they used to call them gods (alihah) and partners (shurakaa), and they would assign to them a portion of their wealth.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 30, verse 41:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Corruption has appeared on the land and the sea﴾. The scholars differed concerning the meaning of corruption (fasad), the land (al-barr) and the sea (al-bahr). Qatadah and al-Suddi said: corruption is shirk (associating partners with God), and it is the greatest of corruptions. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah and Mujahid said: the corruption of the land is the killing of one son of Adam his brother, Qabil killing Habil. And in the sea, it is the king who used to seize every ship by force. It was also said: corruption is drought, scarcity of plants and the loss of blessing. Ibn 'Abbas said something similar, saying: it is the diminishing of blessing because of the deeds of the servants, so that they may repent. Al-Nahhas said: this is the best of what has been said concerning the verse. Also from him (Ibn 'Abbas): that corruption in the sea is the cessation of its game (catch) because of the sins of the children of Adam. 'Ata' said: when rain decreases, diving for pearls decreases there, the fishermen fail, and the creatures of the sea become scarce. Ibn 'Abbas said: when the sky rains, the shells in the sea open, and whatever falls into them from the sky becomes pearls. It was also said: corruption is the slump of prices and scarcity of livelihood. It was also said: corruption is sins, highway robbery and oppression, meaning this deed became an obstacle to crops, cultivation and trade, and all these meanings are close to one another. The land (al-barr) and the sea (al-bahr) are the well-known and famous ones in the language [[In J and K: (in jurisprudence).]] and among people, not what some ascetics said: that the land is the tongue and the sea is the heart, because of the apparentness of what is on the tongue and the hiddenness of what is in the heart. It was also said: the land is the deserts, and the sea is the towns, as said by 'Ikrimah. The Arabs call the cities "seas." Qatadah said: the land refers to the people of the tents (al-'amud), and the sea refers to the people of the villages and the countryside. Ibn 'Abbas said: the land is what is of cities and villages not on a river, and the sea is what is on the bank of a river, and Mujahid said the same, saying: "By God, it is not your sea that is meant here, but every village on flowing water is a sea." Al-Nahhas said concerning its meaning that there are two views. One: drought appeared on the land, that is in the desert and its villages, and in the sea, that is in the cities of the sea, like: ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], meaning the scarcity of rain and the rise of prices appeared. ﴿Because of what the hands of people have earned, that He may let them taste some of what they have done﴾, meaning the punishment for some of what they did, then it was omitted. The other view: that sins appeared, such as highway robbery and oppression, and this is corruption in its literal sense, while the first is figurative, except that it is according to the second answer, so there is in the speech an omission and abbreviation indicated by what follows it, and the meaning is: sins appeared on the land and the sea, so God withheld from them the rain and made their prices high, that He may let them taste the punishment for some of what they did. ﴿So that they may return﴾, that is, so that they may repent. And He said: "some of what they did" because the bulk of the recompense is in the Hereafter. The reading is ﴿liyudhiqahum﴾ with the ya'. Ibn 'Abbas read it with the nun, and it is the reading of al-Sulami, Ibn Muhaysin, Qunbul and Ya'qub, as an expression of magnification, meaning: We let them taste the punishment for some of what they did.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say: "Travel through the land"﴾, meaning: say to them, O Muhammad, "Travel through the land so that they may take warning from those who came before them, and observe what was the end of those who denied the messengers." (﴿Most of them were polytheists﴾), meaning: disbelievers, and so they were destroyed.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 30, verse 43:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So set your face toward the upright religion﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, direct your intention and make your orientation the following of the upright religion, meaning Islam. It has also been said: the meaning is, make the truth clear and be thorough in giving warning, occupy yourself with what you are engaged in, and do not grieve over them.

(Before there comes a Day which will not be turned back from Allah) That is, Allah will not turn it back from them; so when He does not turn it back, no one will be able to repel it. According to other than Sibawayh, it is permissible to say "lā maradda lahu" (there is no turning back for it); but according to Sibawayh this is remote, unless there is a conjunction (ʿatf) in the speech. The intended day is the Day of Resurrection.

(On that Day they will be split apart) Ibn ʿAbbas said: its meaning is that they will scatter. And the poet said:

*And we were like the two boon companions of Judhayma for a period of time, until it was said: "They will never separate."*

[[The verse is by Mutammim ibn Nuwayra al-Yarbuʿi, from a poem in which he mourns his brother Malik, whose opening line is:

*By my life, my time is not a lament for a perished one, nor a grieving over what has befallen and pained me.*

As for his saying "kanadamay Judhayma" (like the two boon companions of Judhayma): this refers to Judhayma al-Abrash, who was a king. His two companions are said to be Malik and ʿAqil, and they are cited as a proverb for the length of their companionship. It is said they kept him company for forty years, and they never repeated a single story to him.]]

That is, they will never part. A parallel to it is His saying: ﴿On that Day they will be divided﴾ [al-Rum: 14], "a group in the Garden and a group in the Blaze." The original form is yataṣaddaʿūn (they will be split apart). It is said: tasaddaʿa al-qawm (the people scattered) when they dispersed, and from it the word ṣudaʿ (headache) is derived, because it splits the sides of the head.

"Whoever disbelieves, upon him is his disbelief" — i.e., the recompense of his disbelief.

(And whoever does righteous deeds, for themselves they prepare [a resting place]) — i.e., they lay down for themselves, in the Hereafter, a bed, a dwelling and a place of settling through righteous deeds. From this comes "mahd al-sabiy" (the cradle of the infant). Al-mihad is the bedding, and I "mahhadtu al-firash mahdan" means I spread the bedding and made it level. Tamhid al-umur (preparing affairs) is arranging and setting them right. Tamhid al-udhr (laying out an excuse) is presenting it and accepting it. Al-tamahhud is becoming firmly established.

Ibn Abi Najih related from Mujahid regarding "for themselves they prepare," that he said: "In the grave."

"His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That He may reward those who believe﴾, meaning: they prepare (a place) for themselves, so that Allah may reward them from His bounty. It was also said: they will be separated (on the Day of Judgment), so that Allah may reward them, that is, so that the disbeliever may be distinguished from the Muslim. ﴿Indeed, He does not love the disbelievers.﴾"

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 30, verse 46:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And among His signs is that He sends the winds as bearers of good tidings﴾, meaning: and among the indications of the perfection of His power is the sending of the winds as bearers of good tidings, that is, of rain, because they precede it. Its explanation has already passed in "al-Hijr" [[See vol. 10, p. 15.]].

(﴿And that He may let you taste of His mercy﴾) meaning the rain and fertility.

(﴿and that the ships may run﴾) i.e. on the sea when the winds blow. He added "by His command" because the winds may blow without being favourable, so it is necessary to anchor the ships and devise ways to hold them back; and sometimes they may blow violently and drown them, by His command.

(﴿and that you may seek of His bounty﴾) meaning sustenance through trade, (﴿so that you may give thanks﴾) for these blessings by affirming the Oneness of God and by obedience. This has all already passed with explanation [[See vol. 1, pp. 388 and 397, and vol. 2, p. 194 onward.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 30, verse 47:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We sent messengers before you to their peoples, and they came to them with clear proofs,﴾

That is, with the miracles (mu'jizat) and the clear evidences (hujaj al-nayyirat).

﴿So We took vengeance,﴾

That is, they disbelieved, so We took vengeance upon those who disbelieved. ﴿And it was ever incumbent upon Us to help the believers.﴾

The word ḥaqqan is in the accusative as the predicate (khabar) of kana, and naṣr is its subject (ism). Abu Bakr used to pause at ḥaqqan, meaning: "And Our punishment was indeed the truth." Then he said: ﴿Upon Us is the help of the believers﴾ is a new sentence (ibtida') and a predicate (khabar). That is, He informed that He does not break the promise (al-mi'ad), and there is no breaking of Our report.

It is narrated from the hadith of Abu al-Darda', who said: I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "There is no Muslim who defends the honour of his brother except that it is incumbent upon Allah, Exalted is He, to ward off from him the Fire of Hell on the Day of Resurrection." Then he recited: ﴿And it was ever incumbent upon Us to help the believers.﴾ [[In manuscripts J and Sh: "That is, We informed of it and ...."]]

This was mentioned by al-Nahhas, al-Tha'labi, al-Zamakhshari and others.

Allah's words: ﴿It is Allah who sends the winds﴾. Ibn Muhayṣin, Ibn Kathir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "al-rīḥ" (the wind) in the singular. The rest read it in the plural. Abu 'Amr said: "Whatever carries the meaning of mercy is plural, and whatever carries the meaning of punishment is singular."

The meaning of this verse, and of others like it, has already been discussed in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 2, p. 197 onward.]].

"Kisafan" is the plural of kisfah (a piece, a fragment). In the reading of al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, 'Abd al-Rahman al-A'raj and Ibn 'Amir, it is read "kisfan" with the sin unvocalized. This too is a plural of kisfah, just as one says sidrah and sidr (a lote tree and lote trees). On this reading, the pronoun that follows refers back to it, meaning: "you see the rain (al-wadq), that is the rain, come out from between the fragments (al-kisaf)." Since every plural whose singular differs from it only by the feminine ending (al-ha') allows the masculine form, the masculine pronoun here is acceptable. Whoever reads "kisafan" with the fatha takes the pronoun to refer to the clouds (al-sahab). In the reading of al-Dahhak, Abu al-'Aliyah and Ibn 'Abbas: "fa-tara al-wadqa yakhruju min khilalihi," and "khilal" may be the plural of "khilal" (gap, opening).

(Then, when He causes it to strike) i.e., with the rain, (whom He wills of His servants, behold, they rejoice) they are glad at the rain falling upon them.

(And although before it was sent down upon them, they had been despairing) i.e., hopeless and downcast, the sorrow evident upon them because the rain was withheld from them. Regarding "min qablihi" (before it), according to al-Akhfash it is a repetition meaning emphasis, and most grammarians hold this view, as reported by al-Nahhas. Qutrub said: the first "qabli" refers to the sending down and the second to the rain, meaning: "and although they were, before the sending down, before the rain." It is also said: the meaning is "before the descent of the rain upon them, before the crops," and the rain indicates the crops since they come about through it. It is also indicated by "then they see it turned yellow," as will come. It is also said: the meaning is "before the clouds, before seeing them," and al-Nahhas chose this view, i.e., before seeing the clouds, "lamublisin" meaning truly despairing. The clouds were already mentioned [[See vol. 2, p. 200 onward.]].

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 30, verse 50:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So look at the traces of Allah's mercy﴾, means the rain. That is, look with an insightful, reflective gaze, meaning: reason from it to the conclusion that the One who has power over it has power over giving life to the dead. Ibn 'Amir, Hafs, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "*āthār*" (traces) in the plural. The rest read it in the singular, because it is in construct with a singular noun. The *athar* (trace, effect) is the subject of *yuhyi* (gives life), and the subject may also be the Name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. As for the one who reads *āthār* in the plural, *raḥmat Allāh* (Allah's mercy) may be intended to indicate multiplicity, as in His saying: ﴿And if you tried to count Allah's favour, you could not enumerate it﴾ [Ibrahim: 34]. See vol. 9, p. 376 onward.

Al-Jahdari, Abu Haywah and others read *kayfa tuhyi al-arḍ* (how it gives life to the earth) with a *tā'* (feminine prefix). They took the feminine form in reference to the word *raḥmah* (mercy), since the trace of mercy stands in its place, so it is as though it were the mercy itself. That is: how does the mercy give life to the earth, or the traces? *Yuhyi* means: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, gives life, or the rain, or the trace, according to whoever reads it with a *yā'* (masculine prefix). The phrase *kayfa yuhyi al-arḍ* is in a position of accusative as a *ḥāl* (circumstantial clause), by interpreting it according to the sense, because the wording is an interrogative while the *ḥāl* is a predicate. The implied meaning is: look at the trace of Allah's mercy, giving life to the earth after its death.

(﴿Indeed, that is the One who gives life to the dead, and He is over all things Competent﴾) This is an inference from the witnessed to the unseen (*istidlāl bi-l-shāhid 'alā al-ghā'ib*).

The Almighty's saying: ﴿And if We send a wind, and they see it turning yellow﴾, meaning the wind. The word for wind may be treated as masculine (tadhkir). Muhammad ibn Yazid said: It is not impermissible to treat any feminine noun that is not a true feminine (ghayr haqiqi) as masculine, as in "a'jabani al-dar" (the house pleased me) and similar constructions. It was also said: "they saw the clouds." Ibn Abbas said: "the crops," which is the trace (al-athar), and the meaning is: they saw the trace turning yellow. The yellowing of the crops after they had turned green indicates their drying out. Likewise, the clouds indicate that they will not rain, and the wind indicates that it will not fertilize. (Then they would continue to disbelieve after it), meaning: indeed they would continue. The use of the past tense in place of the future is acceptable because the sentence carries the sense of a conditional, and a conditional can only take the future. This was said by al-Khalil and others.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 30, verse 52–53:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾, meaning: the proofs have become clear, O Muhammad, but they, because of their habituation to blindly following their forefathers in disbelief, their minds have died and their insight has become blind, so it is not possible for you to make them hear or to guide them. This is a refutation of the Qadariyyah (the group that denies divine predestination).

﴿You can only make hear those who believe in Our signs﴾, meaning: you cannot make the admonitions of Allah heard except by the believers who lend their ears to the evidences of monotheism, and for whom guidance has been decreed. This has passed in "an-Naml" [[See vol. 13, p. 233.]], and the word "bihadi al-'umy" (﴿guide the blind﴾) occurs here without a ya' (i.e., as bihadi rather than bihadi-ya).
